q: A freight forwarder wants to cut the time staff spend answering shipping-exception emails. Replies need the customer's shipment record and the carrier's policy documents, and a staff member must approve each reply before it is sent. Which solution shape best fits?
opts: One augmented call per email with a lookup tool and cached policy text, producing a draft for staff approval
A planner, researcher, writer and reviewer team of agents that negotiate each reply among themselves before staff see it
An autonomous agent that sends replies straight to customers and updates the shipment system once its accuracy looks high
A keyword rules engine that picks one of fifty canned replies per email, which avoids model cost and any need for review
why: The input is varied free text, the needed data is one lookup plus stable policy text, and a person approves the output, so one well-augmented call is the simplest shape that meets the need. A four-agent team adds token overhead and hand-off loss with no context-pollution, parallelism or specialization reason. A fully autonomous agent removes the approval the business requires and adds risk. A canned-reply rules engine cannot handle the variety of real exceptions.

q: A support platform receives billing questions, technical faults and account-closure requests. Each type needs different instructions, tools and escalation rules, and a lightweight classifier can sort incoming messages accurately. Which pattern should the architect choose?
opts: Evaluator-optimizer: draft a reply, have a critic review it, and loop until the draft passes, for every message type
Routing: classify each message first, then dispatch it to a specialized prompt and tool set for its category
Voting: run all three handlers on every message and take the majority answer, so no single handler can be wrong
Orchestrator-workers: let a central model invent subtasks for each message at run time, then merge the replies
why: Distinct categories that can be classified accurately are the textbook case for routing: each handler is tuned for one kind of request, so optimizing for one does not hurt another. Evaluator-optimizer polishes a single output and does not separate categories. Voting triples cost and produces conflicting answers from handlers built for different jobs. Orchestrator-workers is for subtasks that cannot be predicted in advance, which is not the situation here.

q: A migration tool must replace a deprecated library across customer repositories. How many files change, and what each change involves, depends on the repository and cannot be known before the tool inspects it. Which pattern fits best?
opts: Prompt chaining with a fixed list of steps that is applied to every repository in the same order, with a gate after each
Routing by file extension, with one specialized prompt per programming language handling all of that language's files
Sectioning into three pre-defined parallel calls, each given an equal share of the repository's files to rewrite
Orchestrator-workers: a central call inspects the repository, decides the subtasks, and delegates them to worker calls
why: When the subtasks depend on the input and cannot be listed in advance, a central model should decompose the task at run time and delegate, which is orchestrator-workers. A fixed chain or a pre-defined split assumes you already know the structure of the work, and routing by extension only chooses a prompt without deciding how many changes to make.

q: A localization team translates marketing copy in which tone and idiom matter. First drafts often miss nuance, but reviewers can state clear criteria (register, brand terms, idiom) and a second model can apply them. Which pattern improves output quality most directly?
opts: Parallel voting: translate the copy three times and publish whichever wording appears most often across the drafts
Routing: send each target language to a different model and publish that model's first draft after a spell check
Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, another critiques against the criteria, and the loop repeats until it passes
Prompt chaining: draft once, then have a second call reformat the draft to the house style and publish it
why: Evaluator-optimizer fits when criteria are explicit and iterative feedback measurably improves the result, which is exactly translation nuance with a rubric. Voting gives diverse attempts to compare but never refines a draft, routing only picks a model, and a reformatting chain adds no critique.

q: A prototype uses five agents (planner, implementer, tester, reviewer, documenter) to deliver features. Logs show each hand-off losing context, and the team is spending more tokens coordinating than building. What is the best redesign?
opts: Add a sixth coordinator agent whose only job is to manage the hand-offs and summarize each stage for the next agent
Let one agent own a feature together with its tests, and keep a separate agent only for black-box verification
Switch every agent to the strongest model tier, so that fewer details are lost whenever work changes hands
Make all five agents read and write one shared transcript so that nothing is ever lost between the roles
why: Splitting by type of activity (planner, tester, reviewer) is problem-centric decomposition and creates a telephone game in which each recipient lacks the reasoning behind earlier steps. Splitting along context boundaries keeps the building agent's context intact, and a verifier that only runs tests needs little of it. A coordinator adds another hop, a bigger model does not restore lost context, and a shared transcript recreates the bloat the split was meant to avoid.

q: A research assistant must compare twelve vendors against a rubric using public sources. Each vendor can be researched independently, the work is high value, and the final report must synthesize all twelve. Which decomposition is most appropriate?
opts: A role-based pipeline of searcher, summarizer, formatter and reviewer agents that all share one growing transcript
One agent that researches the twelve vendors one after another inside a single conversation, however long it grows
A lead agent that spawns one research subagent per vendor, each in its own context, and synthesizes their findings
One subagent per paragraph of the final report, each writing its paragraph from the full pile of raw research notes
why: Independent research paths are a recommended decomposition boundary: each subagent works in a clean context, can run in parallel, and returns a condensed result so the lead's context stays focused. A role-based pipeline is problem-centric and loses context at each hand-off, a single sequential conversation suffers context pollution as the sources pile up, and splitting by report paragraph cuts across the shared evidence.

q: A lead agent delegates 'fix the failing checkout test' to a subagent, which then spends many turns rediscovering which repository, file and error to look at. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?
opts: The subagent's output limit is too low; raise its max_tokens so that it can keep exploring the codebase for longer
The subagent's model is too small for the task; upgrade it to the same model that the lead agent uses
A subagent inherits none of the parent's conversation; put paths, error output and constraints in the delegation prompt
The subagent needs the lead's full system prompt copied into its own so that it behaves exactly like the lead
why: A subagent starts with a fresh context, and the only thing passed from parent to child is the task prompt, so anything it needs (paths, errors, decisions, constraints) must be written into that prompt. A larger token limit or model does not supply missing facts, and copying the lead's system prompt gives it the lead's role but still none of the task context.

q: A claims-intake system extracts fields from submitted forms and writes them to the core claims system. Adjusters often correct the extracted values, but the team keeps no record of those corrections and accuracy has not improved in months. Which architectural element is missing?
opts: A caching layer in front of the extraction call, so that repeated forms are not processed twice by the model
A second extraction pass at higher effort for every form, with the two results compared before they are written
A larger context window, so that more of the earlier form history fits into each extraction request
A feedback loop that captures adjuster corrections, links them to inputs and prompts, and feeds evaluations
why: The pipeline stops at output, so nothing learns from human corrections. A complete design closes the loop: corrections become labeled examples for evaluation sets and prompt or retrieval changes. Caching, extra passes and a bigger window may change cost or latency but give the team no new information about where the system is wrong.

q: A team will run a nightly agent that processes large document sets for up to two hours using shell and file tools. They want to avoid building a sandbox, an event store and a tool-execution layer, and their data terms allow Anthropic to hold session history. Which option best fits?
opts: The Message Batches API, because the job runs overnight and batch requests cost half as much as standard ones
Claude Managed Agents, with a cloud environment, one session per run and a session budget as a cost ceiling
The Messages API with their own loop, sandbox and persistence, for maximum control over every step of the run
The Agent SDK in containers the team operates, with transcripts persisted to their own database
why: Managed Agents supplies the hosted harness, sandbox, persisted events and long-running sessions, which is what the team wants to avoid building. The Batches API processes independent Messages requests at a discount, not a stateful loop with shell tools. The other two options mean the team operates the loop, sandbox or processes itself, the opposite of the stated goal.

q: An internal developer portal must embed a coding agent with file editing, shell access, permission rules and hooks inside a service the company operates. The team does not want to write the tool loop. Which option fits?
opts: The Claude Agent SDK, embedded in the company's own service so the loop runs in a process the team operates
Claude Managed Agents, because Anthropic should host the agent loop and run the sandbox for the portal
The Messages API with a hand-written agent loop and the team's own tool execution and permission layer
The MCP connector alone, which gives the model tools without any agent loop of its own
why: The Agent SDK packages Claude Code's loop, built-in tools, permissions and hooks as a library that runs in a process you operate, which matches both the embedding requirement and the wish to avoid writing the loop. Managed Agents moves execution to Anthropic-hosted infrastructure rather than the company's service. The raw Messages API leaves the loop to the team, and a connector supplies tools but no loop.

q: A CFO asks how the proposed support assistant's architecture serves the cost and performance-SLA pillars. Which response is strongest?
opts: It uses the largest model for every ticket, so quality risk is minimal and no routing, tuning or monitoring is needed
The chosen model has a low price per million tokens, which is the only cost metric that matters to the business
A multi-agent design is used, which demonstrates transformation and shows leadership how modern the system is
Small model for routine tickets, cached shared prefix, and dashboards for cost per resolved ticket and p95 latency
why: A defensible answer ties specific design decisions to measurable outcomes: routing and caching reduce cost per resolved ticket, and latency is tracked against the service target. Using the largest model everywhere ignores cost, per-token price alone misses turns and retries, and choosing multi-agent for show adds cost without addressing either pillar.

q: A support agent can search the knowledge base, draft replies, issue refunds and close accounts. Refunds above a threshold and account closures are hard to reverse. Where should human approval be placed?
opts: Before every tool call, including knowledge-base searches, so that nothing happens without a person's approval
Before refunds above the threshold and before account closures, while searching and drafting run freely
Nowhere in the flow; the system prompt tells the agent to ask a person whenever it is unsure
After all actions complete, in a weekly review of the logs that flags anything that looks wrong
why: Approval gates belong where the blast radius is large and reversal is hard. Gating every call defeats the automation, relying on the prompt alone leaves a high-impact action to probabilistic behavior, and a weekly log review detects problems after the damage is done.

q: A 40-step data-reconciliation agent sometimes misreads a column mapping at step 3, and every later step then builds on the mistake. Restarting costs hours. Which change best contains the damage?
opts: Raise max_tokens so the agent has more room to reason carefully about each step before it acts
Tell the agent in the prompt to double-check every step twice and to stop if anything looks inconsistent
Add verification checkpoints after milestones, and persist state so a run can resume from the last verified one
Run the same 40 steps in several parallel copies and keep whichever copy finishes first with a result
why: Errors compound in long autonomous runs, so the design needs explicit verification points and durable state to resume from. More tokens and a request to be careful do not create a check that can fail, and racing duplicate runs spends more and can finish first with the same wrong assumption.

q: A regulated insurer's intake process always follows the same six steps (identify policy, extract facts, check coverage rules, compute a summary, flag exceptions, produce a record). Auditors require a deterministic order with each step logged. Which design fits best?
opts: An autonomous agent that plans its own steps for each claim and decides when the intake is complete
A single prompt that performs all six steps in one response and returns the finished record in one go
Orchestrator-workers, where a central model decides at run time which of the steps to run for each claim
A prompt chain with one focused call per step and programmatic gates between them
why: A fixed, auditable sequence is what workflows are for: each step is a focused call, code enforces the order and gates can reject bad intermediate output, and every step is loggable. An autonomous agent or orchestrator makes the order the model's choice, and a single prompt hides the steps and offers no place to check them.

q: A consumer chat feature must screen each user message for policy violations without adding noticeable delay to normal replies. Which design meets both needs?
opts: Screen first, wait for the verdict, and only then start generating the answer to the user's message
Run the screening call and the answering call in parallel, and release the answer only if screening passes
Answer immediately and screen afterwards, retracting the reply if the screen fails once it has been shown
Ask a single call to screen the message and answer it in the same response to save a round trip
why: Sectioning in parallel hides the screening latency behind the answering latency, while the gate keeps unscreened content from reaching the user. Sequential screening adds the full delay, answering first exposes the user to unscreened output, and combining both jobs in one call blurs two tasks that perform better when handled separately.

q: A compliance team must analyze 3,000 policy documents, far more than fit in one context window, and each document can be analyzed independently. Cost matters. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Run one top-tier agent that reads the documents one after another in a single growing conversation
Paste as many documents as fit into one prompt and ignore the rest, since the answer is similar anyway
Lower the effort level of a single agent, since effort alone determines the size of the bill for this job
Partition the documents among lower-cost worker agents coordinated by an orchestrator that merges the results
why: When the work is larger than one window, delegating partitions to lower-cost workers is the pattern that saved money in Anthropic's measurements, because the bill is the reading itself and lowering effort cannot shrink it. One growing conversation hits the window and context rot, and truncating the input silently drops most of the work.

q: An executor on a lower tier stalls only on hard planning decisions, so the team adds a higher-tier model through the advisor tool. Early results show no quality gain, though the advisor definition adds prompt tokens to every request. What should the team check first?
opts: Whether the executor really consults the advisor: measure the consult rate and compare with the executor alone at higher effort
Whether max_tokens is large enough for the advisor's reply to fit, since truncated advice would explain the missing gain
Whether to promote the advisor to be the executor on every turn, since the stronger model would always do better
Whether adding a second advisor from the same tier raises agreement and so gives the executor more confidence
why: An advisor can help only when it is consulted. Measuring the consult rate, and comparing the pairing with the executor alone on its own effort curve, shows whether the tool adds anything for its cost. Promoting the advisor changes the architecture instead of diagnosing it, and the other two options do not address why no consultation benefit appears.

q: Four teams propose multi-agent designs. Which proposal has the strongest justification for using more than one agent?
opts: A three-phase feature build in which each phase depends on the previous phase's full reasoning and decisions
A five-tool FAQ assistant that answers short questions in a single turn, each with a one-line reply
A tightly coupled schema migration whose steps constantly depend on each other's intermediate state
Breadth-first competitive research across thirty independent sources, with findings condensed for a lead
why: Multi-agent designs pay off for independent, parallelizable work whose bulky intermediate output should stay out of the lead's context. Sequential phases that share reasoning, tightly coupled steps and a small single-turn assistant all lose more to coordination than they gain.

q: In Claude Managed Agents, a lead agent must ask a security specialist follow-up questions after the specialist's first report. Which mechanism fits?
opts: A dynamic workflow run, because the threads of a run stay open so that the lead can ask follow-ups
Subagent delegation, because a subagent's thread persists and can receive follow-up messages
An advisor model, because it keeps working on the lead's behalf and can answer questions on demand
Separate sessions, because agents inside one session have no way to send messages to each other
why: A subagent's thread stays available until archived, so the lead can send follow-ups and the subagent retains its earlier turns. The agent cannot message a workflow run's threads, which the server archives at the end of the run. An advisor is consulted for guidance mid-turn by the primary thread and does not hold a work stream, and sessions are not required for agents to coordinate.

q: A scheduled Managed Agents job usually costs a few dollars but occasionally costs ten times that when it loops on a flaky tool. Finance wants a guaranteed ceiling per run. What should the architect configure?
opts: A system prompt instruction telling the agent to stop and report when its costs seem unusually high
A lower max_tokens so each response is shorter and a looping run spends less on every turn
The Batch API discount, which halves the price of every request in the job and so halves the worst case
A session budget on every session or deployment, backed by a workspace spend limit as the final backstop
why: A session budget is a platform-enforced ceiling: at the cap the session pauses rather than spending more. A prompt instruction is only guidance, a smaller output cap neither counts turns nor stops loops, and the Batch API is not available for Managed Agents sessions, which are interactive by design.

q: A contact-center assistant must deliver the first words of an answer within two seconds at the 95th percentile. About 80 percent of questions are simple FAQs; the rest need multi-step lookups. Which configuration best meets the SLA while controlling cost?
opts: Use the highest tier at maximum effort for every question, so that quality never limits the experience
Route FAQs to the small tier at low effort, escalate complex cases, stream responses and cache the static prefix
Run a three-agent debate on every question and return the consensus answer as soon as two agents agree
Send every request through the Batch API for the discount and notify users when their answers are ready
why: Routing matches model and effort to difficulty, streaming improves time to first token and caching shortens prefix processing, so the common case is fast and cheap while hard cases still get capability. The top tier at maximum effort misses the latency target, a debate multiplies latency and tokens, and batch results can take up to a day.

q: Which requirement is the strongest signal that a fixed workflow should give way to a true agent loop?
opts: The task always runs the same five steps in the same order, so the path can be written down in advance
The number and order of steps cannot be predicted and depend on what each tool call returns
Outputs must be reproducible step by step so that an auditor can replay exactly what happened
The request is a single classification with a fixed label set and a known list of examples
why: Agents suit open-ended problems where the path cannot be hard-coded and the model must act on feedback from the environment. The other three describe predictable or auditable work, which a workflow or a single call serves better with less cost and risk.

q: A prototype using one call with retrieval and three examples meets 92 percent of its quality target. The tech lead proposes a multi-agent redesign to close the gap. What is the best next step?
opts: Approve the redesign, because adding more agents always raises accuracy by spreading work across them
Ship at 92 percent without examining the failures, since the prototype is already close to the target
Analyze the failing cases and try targeted fixes, such as retrieval, examples or effort, before adding agents
Move to the smallest tier to free budget for the redesign, then add agents to recover the lost quality
why: The simplest-solution-first principle says to add complexity only when measurements show simpler options fall short. Failure analysis may reveal retrieval or example gaps that are cheaper to fix, and multi-agent systems often use several times the tokens without helping. Shipping blind skips the evidence, and downsizing the model works against the quality goal.

q: A security team requires that the files and processes an agent touches stay on company infrastructure, yet it does not want to operate the agent loop itself. Session history may be stored by Anthropic. Which option fits?
opts: Managed Agents with the default cloud sandbox, because Anthropic manages the container for each session
The Messages API with a loop hosted on company servers, with tools executed inside the company network
Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox on company infrastructure, so tools and files stay in-house
The Agent SDK in company-operated containers, with the company running every session's agent loop
why: A self-hosted sandbox keeps tool execution and the filesystem on infrastructure the company controls while Anthropic still hosts the loop, though session history and tool inputs and outputs still go to Anthropic. The cloud sandbox moves files off site, and the other two satisfy residency but make the team operate the loop. If no conversation data may leave, the Agent SDK or Messages API on a platform the company controls would become the answer instead.

q: A lead agent's answer quality drops after it delegates web research: each subagent returns its full 40,000-token browsing transcript. What design change is best?
opts: Enlarge the lead's context window so that all the returned browsing transcripts can fit in it
Remove the subagents and have the lead run every search itself, which avoids any hand-off between agents
Ask the subagents to compress their transcripts into denser formatting before returning them to the lead
Have each subagent return a short structured finding with sources, keeping raw material in its own context
why: The purpose of delegation is context isolation: helpers should explore widely and return a condensed result, often only one or two thousand tokens, so the lead's window holds signal. Returning raw transcripts defeats it. A bigger window does not stop context rot, and doing all searches in the lead's context creates exactly the pollution the subagents were meant to prevent.

q: A three-hour research run fails after two hours because a tool times out, and the system restarts the entire run from the beginning. Which change gives the best resilience?
opts: Retry the whole run automatically until it succeeds, with a pause between attempts to let the tool recover
Persist progress at checkpoints so a run resumes where it stopped, and report tool failures to the model
Shorten the prompt so the run finishes faster and is less likely to meet a tool timeout
Silently remove the failing tool and let the agent carry on with whatever other tools it has left
why: Agents are stateful and long running, so restarts are expensive and the design should make resumption normal. Telling the model when a tool is failing lets it adapt, for example by trying another source. Blind full retries waste hours, a shorter prompt does not address failures, and silently dropping a tool hides a capability gap from both the model and the operators.

q: One prompt asks the model to extract entities from a letter, classify the risk, and draft a response letter. Quality is uneven across the three tasks. Which change most directly addresses this?
opts: Add 'be careful and thorough' to the prompt so the model gives each of the three tasks equal attention
Move all the instructions to the end of the user message, where the model pays the most attention
Increase max_tokens so that the model has enough room to complete all three tasks in one response
Split the work into a chain of focused calls with a programmatic check between steps
why: Decomposing a complex task into a chain makes each call easier and lets code verify intermediate results, trading a little latency for accuracy. Exhortations, instruction placement and a larger output cap do not change the fact that three different jobs compete inside one call.

q: Which two observations suggest a single agent has outgrown its design and a multi-agent split may be justified? (Choose two.)
opts: The work has three sequential phases that all depend on the same detailed reasoning from earlier steps
Independent subtasks, such as researching separate sources, could run at the same time
The agent handles short questions in a single turn using four well-described tools
Bulky intermediate results from one subtask are crowding out the context needed for later subtasks
The team would like each job title in the process (planner, tester, reviewer) to have its own prompt
why: Context pollution and parallelizable independent work are two of the three situations in which several agents consistently beat one (the third is specialization of tools or instructions). A small single-turn assistant has nothing to split, sequential phases that share reasoning lose context at every hand-off, and sophistication is not a requirement.

q: Which two are good reasons to use a dedicated verification subagent? (Choose two.)
opts: It can judge the result fairly only after reading the builder's complete reasoning history
Verification needs little context from the builder, so the hand-off loses almost nothing
It roughly halves the token cost of the overall task by sharing the builder's context
It enforces an explicit checkpoint using tools such as a test runner or a schema validator
It removes the need to define success criteria, because the verifier decides what good looks like
why: A verifier can black-box test an artifact against stated criteria, so it avoids the telephone-game losses of other splits and gives the workflow a hard checkpoint with the right tools. It does not need the builder's history, it adds a call rather than halving cost, and it works only if success criteria are defined.

q: Which two actions in an order-handling agent most clearly warrant an approval gate? (Choose two.)
opts: Looking up the shipping status of an order for a customer who asked
Refunding an order for an amount above a set monetary threshold
Drafting a reply that a person will review before it is sent
Deleting a customer account together with all of its stored data
Searching the help center for an article that answers the question
why: Gates belong on actions that are costly or hard to reverse: large refunds and permanent deletions. Reads and drafts that a person reviews are low-impact and easily undone, so gating them only slows the flow.

q: Which three conditions favor a predefined workflow over an autonomous agent? (Choose three.)
opts: The problem is open-ended and the path cannot be hard-coded
The steps are known in advance and rarely change
Auditors need a deterministic, logged order of steps
The number of steps depends on what each tool call returns
Predictable latency and cost matter more than flexibility
why: Workflows give predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks. When the number of steps depends on tool results or the path cannot be hard-coded, the model must direct the process, which is what an agent is for.

q: A board paper must map the claims assistant's metrics to the business value pillars. Which two pairings are sound? (Choose two.)
opts: Number of prompt templates written by the team, mapped to transformation
Average handle time per claim before and after launch, mapped to efficiency
Number of staff trained on the new tool, mapped to performance SLAs
p95 response time against the contractual target, mapped to performance SLAs
Parameter count of the selected model, mapped to cost control
why: Handle time measures efficiency and latency against the contractual target measures performance. Counting templates or model parameters measures effort or size rather than business outcomes, and training numbers say nothing about meeting a response-time commitment.

q: Which two statements about delegation in Claude Managed Agents are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Delegated agents can themselves delegate to further agents to any depth, with no limit on threads
Each delegated agent runs in its own session thread with its own conversation history
A delegated agent automatically starts with the lead agent's full conversation history in its context
Agents in a session share the same sandbox filesystem and vault credentials
The lead can send follow-up messages to the threads of a workflow run after it finishes
why: Threads isolate each agent's context, but the agents share the sandbox and credentials, which is a reason to give delegated agents narrow toolsets. Delegated agents do not inherit the lead's conversation, workflow-run threads cannot receive follow-ups and are archived when the run ends, and delegation is limited to one level deep with a cap on child threads.

q: Which two measures best contain compounding errors in a long autonomous run? (Choose two.)
opts: A larger max_tokens on every call, so each step has room to explain its reasoning in more detail
Verification checkpoints after each milestone, so a bad assumption is caught before later steps build on it
Removing turn limits and stop conditions so that the loop has time to recover from its own mistakes
A final pass that repeats the whole chain from scratch and publishes whichever result arrives first
Durable, resumable state so that a failed run restarts from its last verified point instead of the start
why: Checkpoints catch a bad assumption early and durable state avoids paying for the whole run again. Output limits do not detect errors, removing stop conditions invites runaway loops, and an unchecked repeat run can carry the same mistake.

q: Anthropic's guidance for agentic systems is to start with the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
opts: True
False
why: Agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, so a single optimized call with retrieval and examples is often enough, and workflows or agents are added when measurements show the need.

q: In a workflow the model decides which steps to run next, whereas in an agent the steps are fixed in code in advance.
opts: True
False
why: It is the other way around. In a workflow, code paths are predefined and the LLM fills steps in them; in an agent, the model directs its own process and tool use.

q: Multi-agent systems typically use fewer total tokens than a single agent doing the same task.
opts: True
False
why: Duplicated context, coordination messages and result summaries make multi-agent systems use several times more tokens, 3 to 10 times in Anthropic's testing and about 15 times a chat in its research system. They are justified only when the extra thoroughness is worth that cost.

q: A subagent automatically inherits the full conversation history of the agent that spawned it.
opts: True
False
why: A subagent starts with a fresh context. Apart from its own instructions, the only thing the parent passes is the task prompt, so needed facts must be written into it.

q: Having the agent that implements a feature also write that feature's tests is an example of context-centric decomposition.
opts: True
False
why: The implementing agent already holds the context the tests need. Splitting at context boundaries, rather than by type of activity, avoids lossy hand-offs.

q: A verification subagent usually needs the builder's full reasoning history to do its job.
opts: True
False
why: Verification can be done black-box: the verifier needs the artifact, the success criteria and tools to check them, which is why it avoids the telephone-game losses of other splits.

q: A Claude Managed Agents session budget is enforced by the platform, whereas a system prompt asking the agent to save money is only guidance.
opts: True
False
why: At the budget the session pauses with stop reason budget_reached. A prompt instruction depends on the model's behavior and gives no guarantee, so use platform limits where cost or consequences matter.

q: With the Messages API your code owns the tool-use loop, whereas Claude Managed Agents runs the loop on Anthropic's infrastructure.
opts: True
False
why: The Messages API gives direct model access and leaves the loop, tool execution and state to you (the SDK's tool runner can drive the loop in your process). Managed Agents is a hosted harness that runs them for you.

q: Claude Managed Agents is currently eligible for zero data retention and for HIPAA business associate agreement coverage.
opts: True
False
why: Because sessions are stateful and store history, sandbox state and outputs server-side, Managed Agents is not currently eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA BAA coverage. You can delete sessions and uploaded files yourself.

q: The evaluator-optimizer pattern works best when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative feedback measurably improves the output.
opts: True
False
why: The two signs of a good fit are that responses visibly improve with articulated feedback and that a model can supply that feedback. Without clear criteria the loop adds cost and no quality.

q: In Claude Managed Agents, the lead agent can send follow-up messages to the threads of a dynamic workflow run after the run finishes.
opts: True
False
why: The agent cannot send follow-up messages to a run's threads, and the server archives each thread by the end of the run. Use delegated helpers when follow-ups are needed.

q: The main benefit of running research subagents in parallel is coverage and thoroughness, not necessarily a shorter total runtime.
opts: True
False
why: Parallel agents explore more of a large information space, but total computation rises and multi-agent runs can take longer overall than a single agent. The trade is more tokens for broader, more comprehensive results.

q: After enabling prompt caching on a support assistant, the team sees cache reads near zero and a higher bill than before. The system prompt opens with a line giving the current date and time, followed by 10,000 tokens of policy text. What is the best fix?
opts: Extend the cache lifetime to one hour so that the changing prefix is retained for longer between requests
Add a second breakpoint after the policy text so the policy is cached separately from the timestamp line
Move the timestamp into the newest user turn, after the last breakpoint, so the policy prefix is identical each time
Disable caching, since a changing timestamp makes caching impossible for this kind of assistant
why: Cache matching is an exact prefix match, so a value that changes on every request at the front turns each request into a full cache write and never a read, which can cost more than no caching. Moving the volatile text after the last breakpoint restores a stable prefix. A longer lifetime cannot help a prefix that never matches, a breakpoint after the timestamp caches different content each time, and disabling caching forfeits the savings that are available.

q: Analysts query a research assistant, built on Claude Opus 5.5, that carries a 60,000-token reference prefix. In a typical session, nearly every question follows a pause of 8 to 20 minutes while the analyst reads and thinks. Which caching setup is most cost-effective?
opts: The default five-minute lifetime, because every cache read refreshes the entry at no charge
The one-hour cache lifetime on the prefix, written once and reused across the session's pauses
The default lifetime plus keep-alive requests every four minutes to stop the entry from expiring
No caching, because pauses of this length make cache reads unlikely to be worth the write premium
why: Gaps longer than five minutes expire the default cache, so each question would pay the write price again. The one-hour lifetime costs more to write but survives the pauses, so most turns read the prefix cheaply. On Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, keep-alive requests were measured to cost more than the one-hour option when pauses come before nearly every turn and run long, and skipping caching gives up the discount entirely.

q: A retailer must classify two million support tickets a day into forty categories. Labels can be checked against a hand-labeled set, and responses must return within a second or two. Which model strategy is most appropriate?
opts: Start with the most capable tier to be safe, then optimize for cost once the system is in production
Use the most capable tier with fast mode for every ticket so that responses are quick and accurate
Choose the model with the lowest published price per token and skip evaluation to save engineering time
Start with the small, fast tier, measure accuracy on the labeled set, and move up only if a gap remains
why: High-volume, latency-sensitive classification with checkable outputs is the use case the smallest tier is positioned for, and an evaluation set makes the upgrade decision evidence-based. Starting at the top tier or adding fast mode pays a large premium for capability the task may not need, and selecting by price alone without measuring quality risks both accuracy and rework.

q: A research agent runs for hours on difficult analysis. On the team's evaluations, Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh and max effort still misses the quality target. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Move to Claude Haiku 5.5 at high effort, which saves cost and is likely to reach the same quality
Enable fast mode, which raises output speed and should also lift the quality of the results
Evaluate Claude Fable 5.1, the more capable tier, on the same evaluations before deciding
Accept the result, because effort above high does not change quality on difficult analysis
why: Anthropic suggests moving to the top tier for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work when evaluations on the tier below at higher effort still fall short, and measuring the result on the same suite. Dropping to the smallest tier moves the wrong way, fast mode changes output speed rather than capability, and the effort ceiling claim is not true: higher effort can change results, which is why you sweep it.

q: An agent on the Opus tier meets its quality target in evaluations but is slower and more expensive than the budget allows. What should the architect try first?
opts: Switch immediately to the smallest tier, since it is the cheapest and fastest option and the evaluations probably still pass
Sweep lower effort levels on the same model against the evaluations, keeping the cheapest that holds quality
Raise max_tokens so that tasks finish in fewer turns, which should cut the total cost of each task
Delete the system prompt to cut input tokens on every request, then rely on the model's defaults
why: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost inside one model and is often a better lever than changing models, so sweep two or three levels on real traffic and keep the cheapest one that holds quality. Jumping tiers skips that evidence, and the other options neither target thinking cost nor preserve behavior.

q: Model A costs 60 percent less per token than Model B. In the team's agent evaluation, Model A needs about three times as many turns and solves fewer tasks. How should the team compare the two?
opts: By the published price per million input tokens, since that is the figure on the pricing page
By cost per completed task, using each model's measured turns and success rate
By the size of the context window, since a larger window lets one request carry more of the work
By output speed alone, since the faster model finishes the evaluation and so costs less
why: You pay for completed tasks, not tokens. A cheaper model that takes more turns and fails more often can cost more per solved task, and tokenizer changes can distort per-token comparisons between generations. Context size and raw speed matter only to the extent they change that unit cost or the latency budget.

q: A newer Claude model has been released, and the team wants to move a production agent to it. Which approach is best practice?
opts: Swap the model ID everywhere in one release and watch the support channel for complaints
Keep every prompt untouched, because a newer model always reads old prompts exactly as the old one did
Wait until the old model is retired, then switch every workload to the new one in a single step
Audit the prompts, run the evaluations, check for rejected parameters, and shadow a slice of traffic first
why: Each generation responds to prompts differently: older text such as 'verify twice' can be obeyed literally, some parameters are rejected by newer models, and the change should be measured on your own workload before full cutover. Swapping blindly, assuming equivalence, or waiting for a retirement deadline all skip that evidence and leave no safe time to fix regressions.

q: After moving a support agent to a newer model, cost per ticket rose with no gain in accuracy. The prompt still says 'verify every figure twice', 'be maximally thorough', and includes a hand-written scratchpad section. What is the best action?
opts: Add stronger wording so the model knows that the verification and thoroughness instructions really matter, then re-test
Audit the prompt for the new model, rewrite or remove the over-literal and redundant instructions, then re-evaluate
Lower max_tokens so that the extra tool rounds are cut off before they add cost to each ticket
Permanently revert to the old model, since the new one is evidently worse for this workload
why: Newer models follow instructions written for older ones more literally, which produces extra tool rounds and writing, and a hand-made scratchpad can conflict with the model's own thinking. A prompt audit is a free win that lowers cost and can restore accuracy. Stronger wording makes it worse, a smaller output cap truncates work instead of removing the cause, and reverting gives up the upgrade.

q: A triage prompt classifies emails as urgent, routine or spam. The instructions are clear, yet borderline emails get inconsistent labels from run to run. Which is the most appropriate first change?
opts: Restate the definitions in a new paragraph with the word IMPORTANT in capitals so that the model weighs them more
List every conceivable edge case as a separate rule in the system prompt so nothing is left to inference
Switch to a larger model before changing anything else, since consistency comes from capability
Add three to five diverse, tagged examples that include borderline emails with the intended labels
why: Well-chosen examples are among the most reliable ways to steer judgment and consistency: they should be relevant, diverse and wrapped in tags so they are not confused with instructions. A laundry list of edge-case rules is the pattern Anthropic advises against, emphasis does not add information, and a larger model is a costlier step to try only after cheap prompt fixes.

q: A pipeline passes model output to a billing system that rejects any schema violation. Occasionally a required field is missing or a number arrives as text, despite a prompt saying 'always return valid JSON'. Which change provides a guarantee?
opts: Use structured outputs, with a JSON schema in output_config.format or strict tool use, to constrain decoding
Strengthen the prompt: 'You MUST return valid JSON and never omit a field', and repeat it at the end
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so the model has no choice but to continue in JSON
Parse leniently with a regular expression and fill any missing fields with sensible default values
why: Structured outputs constrain generation to the schema, so the result is always parseable and correctly typed without retries. Prompt wording is guidance, not a guarantee. Prefilled assistant turns are not supported on recent models and return an error, and silently defaulting missing values hides data-quality problems from a system that needs correct data.

q: A team tells a recent model to 'think step by step inside thinking tags and show your reasoning'. Responses are sometimes declined, and outputs are longer and costlier. What is the best change?
opts: Keep the instruction as written and increase max_tokens so the reasoning has room to be written out in full
Prefill the response with an opening thinking tag so that the model starts its reasoning in the right place
Rely on built-in adaptive thinking at a suitable effort, and ask only for the answer and a brief justification
Add an instruction that the model must never reason before answering so the outputs are short and cheap
why: Current models reason internally through adaptive thinking, steered by effort, and prompts that ask for reasoning to be written out in the response can be declined as reasoning-extraction requests. Asking for the answer plus a short justification keeps outputs auditable. A larger limit does not address the refusals, prefill is not supported on recent models, and forbidding reasoning would hurt quality.

q: A long-running agent accumulates large raw search results that are no longer needed once read, but its earlier decisions and plans must remain word for word. Which lever fits best?
opts: Tool result clearing through context editing: old results go, and the rest of the history stays intact
Server-side compaction of the whole conversation into a summary, which keeps the gist of every earlier step
Starting a fresh conversation on every turn and re-sending only the most recent user message each time
Raising the context window limit so that the accumulated search results no longer cause any pressure
why: Context editing can clear stale tool results by rule while keeping decisions verbatim; clearing a worthwhile amount at a time limits cache rewrites. Compaction summarizes everything, which can blur details that must stay exact, a fresh conversation each turn discards state, and a larger limit leaves the clutter that causes context rot.

q: A coding agent works on one project across many days and starts each session with a fresh context window. It repeatedly rediscovers decisions it made earlier. What is the best design?
opts: Rely on the one-million-token window to hold the transcripts of every earlier session in a single context
Paste the full previous transcript into the first message of each session so the model sees what happened
Keep progress notes, test status and a decision log in files that it reads at the start of each session
Ask the user to restate past decisions at the start of each session so that the model has fresh context
why: Persisted notes and state files let an agent recover context quickly and keep the window focused, an approach Anthropic recommends for work spanning many windows. A big window does not carry state across separate sessions, pasting whole transcripts wastes tokens and invites context rot, and making the user repeat decisions pushes the cost onto people.

q: An analyst asks questions over six long contracts totalling about 120,000 tokens. Answers often miss relevant clauses. The prompt currently puts the question first, then the contracts. What is the best restructuring?
opts: Keep the question first and repeat it after each contract so that the model never loses sight of the task
Summarize each contract to one paragraph before sending, so that the model only has to read short inputs
Move the contracts into the system prompt and keep the question first in the user message as before
Put the contracts first in document tags with sources, the question last, and ask for relevant quotes first
why: For long inputs, placing the documents near the top and the query at the end improves quality, tagging documents with sources keeps them distinct, and asking for quotes first helps the model focus on the relevant parts. Repeating the question adds noise, a one-paragraph summary discards the clauses the analyst needs, and moving the contracts to the system prompt does not fix the ordering.

q: An enterprise has forty specialized procedures (expense policy, audit steps, brand voice and others), and any single request needs only one or two. Which reuse mechanism keeps context small and the procedures maintainable, assuming the platform supports it?
opts: One long system prompt containing every procedure, so that the model can always find the relevant one
Agent Skills, whose names and descriptions are always loaded and whose instructions load only on demand
All the procedures appended to every user message, with the relevant ones marked in capital letters
A memory file that the agent must reread in full on every turn before it starts any task
why: Skills use progressive disclosure: only the name and description occupy context until a task triggers a skill, so many can be installed at little cost, and each is a maintainable unit. The other options load every procedure on every request, spending tokens, diluting attention and making updates harder.

q: A multi-tenant assistant has global instructions, a per-tenant policy that changes about daily, and a fresh user question on each request. Which prompt order and breakpoints give the most cache reuse?
opts: User question first, then the tenant policy, then the global instructions, with one breakpoint at the end
Tenant policy first, then the global instructions and the user question, with a breakpoint at the end
Global instructions with a breakpoint, then the tenant policy with a second breakpoint, then the question
Global instructions and the user question together in the system prompt, with one breakpoint after both
why: Caching matches an exact prefix, so the most stable content goes first. Marking the end of the global block lets every tenant share it, a second breakpoint at the end of the tenant policy lets a tenant's requests share that part, and the changing question comes last. The other orders put changing content ahead of stable content, which breaks the prefix and wastes the shared parts.

q: A long, heavily cached conversation needs a new instruction at turn 30. Editing the top-level system prompt would invalidate the cache from that point. On a model that supports it, what is the best approach?
opts: Rewrite the top-level system field with the new instruction, accepting the cache miss from that point onwards on every request
Append a system-role message carrying the new instruction to the messages array, leaving the cached prefix alone
Start a new conversation and resend the whole history as one long user message with the instruction
Add the new instruction to the tool definitions, where it will be read before the conversation
why: A mid-conversation system message leaves the cached prefix unchanged, so only the appended message is processed as new input. Editing the top-level field, restarting with repackaged history, or changing tool definitions all alter earlier content and force the cache to be rewritten.

q: A refund assistant's system prompt says 'NEVER approve a refund over $500'. An auditor asks for assurance that the limit cannot be exceeded, even under unusual or adversarial input. Which design gives it?
opts: Restate the limit three times in the prompt, in capitals, and add the reason it matters to the business
Add ten examples of declined large refunds so that the model recognizes the pattern in adversarial input
Upgrade to a more capable model that follows instructions more reliably under unusual or hostile input
Enforce the limit in the refund tool or back end by rejecting any request over $500
why: A limit enforced in code holds regardless of what the model says, which is what an assurance requires. Repetition, examples and a stronger model all make the desired behavior more likely but remain probabilistic. Where consequences are severe, programmatic enforcement beats prompt-based guidance.

q: A team's 6,000-word system prompt is a thicket of if-then rules that sometimes contradict one another, and behavior changes unpredictably whenever a rule is added. What is the best redesign?
opts: Add more rules to cover each failure as it appears, ordering them by importance so that the key rules win
Rewrite it at the right altitude: role, goals, a few heuristics and canonical examples, with conflicts removed and tested
Replace it with a one-sentence role statement and rely on the model to infer the rest of the behavior
Move all the rules into the user message, where the model weighs them more heavily than in a system prompt
why: Brittle, hard-coded logic and vague one-liners are the two failure modes; the effective middle is specific enough to guide behavior yet flexible enough to give the model heuristics, with canonical examples and tests. More rules deepen the contradictions, a single sentence supplies too little signal, and relocating the same rules changes nothing.

q: A batch feature sometimes fails with a 'prompt is too long' error because customers upload documents of widely varying size. Which approach prevents these failures most reliably?
opts: Catch the error and retry the identical request after a short delay, in case the document size was a glitch
Raise max_tokens so that the model has more room, which stops the input from being treated as too long
Estimate size as characters divided by four and trust that estimate for every file regardless of content
Count tokens before sending, then chunk, truncate with a notice, or route oversized inputs elsewhere
why: The token counting endpoint reports what a request would use, so oversized inputs can be handled deliberately before they fail. Retrying an identical request fails identically, max_tokens limits output rather than input, and character-based estimates drift, especially as tokenizers change between model generations.

q: An agent's cost is dominated by long final reports that users barely read, and every token it writes also re-enters the context on later turns. Which change reduces cost most directly?
opts: Instruct the model to produce the short answer the user will actually read, in a defined format
Lower max_tokens so that long reports are cut off at the limit before they grow too expensive
Set the highest effort level so that the model writes its reports more efficiently and concisely
Add more cache breakpoints to the report text so that repeated report tokens are billed at a lower rate
why: Output tokens cost several times input tokens on the current tiers and are re-read as input on later turns, so asking for the answer you will read is the direct lever. max_tokens is invisible to the model, so lowering it truncates rather than economizes, higher effort tends to spend more rather than less, and breakpoints affect how input is billed, not how much is generated.

q: Which two changes can break a prompt cache and force the prefix to be rewritten? (Choose two.)
opts: Appending a new user message after the last cache breakpoint in the request
Editing the wording of a tool's description in the tools array of the request
Reading the cached prefix again before its lifetime ends, which only refreshes the entry
Putting a per-request timestamp ahead of the stable system text in the prompt
Sending a byte-identical request twice in a row, from the same workspace
why: The cache is an exact prefix match in the order tools, system, messages, so a change to a tool definition or a volatile value placed early invalidates everything after it. New content after the last breakpoint, repeated reads inside the lifetime and identical requests all leave the cached prefix intact (reads even refresh it at no charge).

q: Which two tasks are the best fit for starting with the smallest, fastest model tier? (Choose two.)
opts: Multi-hour autonomous research where evaluations on lower tiers keep failing
High-volume classification whose labels can be checked against a labeled set
One-off, high-stakes analysis whose errors cannot be verified before use
Routing and extraction steps in a pipeline where latency and price matter most
Tasks that demand the highest available reasoning capability
why: The small tier is positioned for high-volume, latency-sensitive classification, extraction and routing, especially when outputs are easy to check so the team can verify quality cheaply. Long-horizon research that lower tiers keep failing, unverifiable high-stakes work and top-capability reasoning point toward stronger tiers.

q: Which three practices make few-shot examples effective? (Choose three.)
opts: Include every edge case you can think of so nothing is left to inference
Make the examples mirror the real task, including its inputs and its output format
Vary the examples so the model does not latch onto an incidental pattern
Use one strong example repeated with small wording changes to reinforce the pattern
Wrap the examples in tags so they are not confused with instructions
why: Relevant, diverse, clearly delimited examples work best, typically three to five. A laundry list of edge cases is the pattern Anthropic advises against in favor of curated canonical examples, and near-duplicates teach the model an unintended pattern.

q: Which two levers keep a long-running agent's context from filling with stale material? (Choose two.)
opts: Lowering the effort level so the model writes less per turn
Clearing old tool results by rule through context editing
Enabling streaming so tokens are delivered as they are generated
Raising max_tokens so each turn can carry more material
Server-side compaction that summarizes older turns
why: Context editing removes stale tool results by rule and compaction replaces older turns with a summary, so both reduce what the window carries. Effort, streaming and the output cap change how much is generated or how it is delivered, not how much history accumulates.

q: Which two items belong in the stable, cacheable prefix of a request? (Choose two.)
opts: The current date and time, added to every request for context
Standing system instructions and policy text shared by all requests
The user's newest question, appended at the end of the conversation
Tool definitions that do not change between requests
Chunks retrieved for this specific request from the knowledge base
why: The prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages, and only content that is identical across requests can be read from the cache. Timestamps, the newest question and per-request retrieved chunks change every time, so they belong after the last breakpoint.

q: Writing a prefix to the prompt cache costs more than ordinary input tokens, while reading it back costs only a fraction of ordinary input.
opts: True
False
why: A five-minute write is billed at a premium (1.25 times base input) and a one-hour write at 2 times, but reads cost a small fraction of base input, generally a tenth and less on some models, so a prefix pays for itself after about one reuse.

q: Lowering max_tokens makes the model write shorter, more economical answers.
opts: True
False
why: The model cannot see max_tokens. A low value simply cuts the response off at the limit, wasting the tokens already generated. To shorten answers, ask for shorter answers in the prompt or use effort, which the model can see.

q: On the newest Claude models, a fixed thinking budget set with budget_tokens is the way to control thinking cost.
opts: True
False
why: Manual thinking budgets are rejected with an error on the newest models. Adaptive thinking decides how much to think, steered by the effort setting, with max_tokens as a hard ceiling on total output.

q: Current Claude model IDs are pinned snapshots, so behavior under an ID does not change until you deliberately switch to a different ID.
opts: True
False
why: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot. That is why an upgrade is a deliberate change that should be preceded by a prompt audit and an evaluation run.

q: Changing the top-level effort value between requests in a cached conversation leaves the cached message prefix intact.
opts: True
False
why: A change to the top-level effort setting invalidates the cached messages (and, on some models, earlier blocks too). Hold effort constant within a conversation that depends on cache hits, or use a per-message effort change on models that support it.

q: For prompts with long documents, placing the documents above the question generally improves response quality.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic advises putting long-form data near the top, above the query and instructions, with the query at the end, which improved quality by up to 30 percent in tests on multi-document inputs.

q: Anthropic's guidance is to compare models on cost per completed task rather than on price per token.
opts: True
False
why: A stronger model can finish a task with fewer turns, and different tokenizers change token counts for the same text, so per-token comparisons mislead. Measure spend and success together on your own workload.

q: Few-shot prompting works best when the examples try to cover every possible edge case, so the model never has to generalize.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic recommends a small set of diverse, canonical examples rather than a laundry list of edge cases. Examples are pictures worth many instructions, but an exhaustive list bloats the prompt and still cannot be complete.

q: Prefilling the assistant turn is still the recommended way to force JSON output on the newest Claude models.
opts: True
False
why: Models from the 4.6 generation onward reject a prefilled final assistant turn with an error. Use structured outputs or strict tool use to guarantee a schema, or direct instructions for lighter needs.

q: A support agent is configured with sixty tools covering CRM, billing, HR and facilities. Tool-selection errors are rising and every request carries a very large block of tool definitions. Support staff only ever need CRM and billing lookups. What is the best change?
opts: Switch to a larger model so that it can choose reliably among sixty tools, whatever the support staff ask for and however many definitions are in the request
Scope the agent to the CRM and billing tools it needs, and load rarely used definitions on demand with tool search
Keep all the tools and add a system prompt line telling the agent to choose carefully between similar tools
Shorten every tool description to a single word to save tokens, since the tool names already say what they do
why: This is capability bloat: the agent holds tools its role never needs, which inflates context, blurs selection and widens the blast radius. Removing the irrelevant domains and deferring the rest fixes the cause. A bigger model still sees the clutter, a prompt line is guidance only, and one-word descriptions make selection worse, because descriptions are the main factor in choosing the right tool.

q: An analytics assistant connects to a data-platform MCP server that exposes forty tools, including delete_dataset and share_publicly. The assistant should only read and query, and the vendor adds new tools every month. Which configuration is best?
opts: Leave every tool enabled and instruct the assistant in the prompt never to delete or share any dataset
Denylist delete_dataset and share_publicly and leave everything else enabled, including new tools as they arrive
Enable everything but log all calls for later review, so any misuse is detected and can be reversed
Disable all tools by default in the toolset and enable only the named read and query tools
why: An allowlist removes every capability the role does not need, including tools the vendor adds later, so risk is eliminated instead of watched. A denylist silently turns on each new tool, a prompt instruction is only guidance, and logging detects misuse after the fact. Removal beats monitoring when a role never needs a capability.

q: A team has attached five MCP servers totaling about 180 tools. Each request carries tens of thousands of tokens of definitions, and the model sometimes picks the wrong tool. Typical tasks use three to five tools. Which change best reduces baseline context and keeps selection accurate?
opts: Rely on prompt caching alone, since cached tokens no longer occupy the context window or influence selection
Raise max_tokens so the model has enough room to think carefully about the full list of 180 tool definitions
Mark the tools as deferred and add the tool search tool so that definitions load only when they are found
Drop three of the five servers at random and accept that some capabilities will no longer be available
why: Tool search with deferred loading keeps only the search tool and a few discovered definitions in context, typically cutting definition tokens by over 85 percent while selection stays accurate across large catalogs. Caching lowers the price of repeated tokens but they still fill the window and still crowd the choice. An output limit does not touch input, and random removal risks dropping needed capability.

q: An agent keeps calling search_orders when it should call get_order. Both tools have one-line descriptions: 'Orders' and 'Order'. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Rename the tools so that the intended one sorts first alphabetically in the list of definitions
Add a system prompt line saying always to prefer get_order, and list the questions that each tool should answer
Rewrite both descriptions: what each does, when to use it and when not to, its parameters and what it does not return
Lower the effort level so that the model deliberates less and is less likely to call the wrong tool
why: Detailed descriptions are the single biggest factor in tool selection. Stating when to use each tool, and what it does not return, resolves look-alike confusion at its source. Alphabetical order has no effect on choice, a prompt line patches one symptom and bypasses the tool contract, and less deliberation makes confusion more likely.

q: A production service on Kubernetes calls the Claude API with a key stored in a cluster secret that has never been rotated. Security wants to remove long-lived secrets from the cluster. Which approach best meets that goal?
opts: Rotate the same key monthly with a scheduled job that updates the cluster secret and restarts the pods
Base64-encode the key inside the secret so that it cannot be read by anyone browsing the cluster
Use Workload Identity Federation: swap the pod's projected service-account token for a short-lived Claude token
Bake the key into the container image so it never appears in cluster configuration or deployment manifests
why: Federation replaces a static secret with a short-lived token exchanged from an identity the workload already has, so there is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate. Rotation shortens exposure but a static key remains, encoding is not protection, and embedding the key in an image spreads it to every place the image goes.

q: An MCP server receives a user's access token and forwards the same token to an internal HR API, which accepts it. A reviewer flags a security gap. What is the gap and the right fix?
opts: The token should be sent over HTTP/2 instead, which encrypts the forwarded value more strongly in transit
The token's lifetime is too short, so the server should request longer-lived tokens and cache them upstream
The upstream call should log the full token value so that any misuse can be traced back to its user
This is token passthrough: accept only tokens issued for this server and use a separate credential upstream
why: MCP forbids token passthrough. A server must validate that an inbound token was issued for it (audience binding) and, when calling other services, act as its own client with a separate token. Forwarding the client's token lets any service that trusts it be reached with the wrong authority, defeats scoping and corrupts audit trails. Transport version, longer lifetimes and logging credentials do not address that, and logging tokens creates a new leak.

q: A team's remote MCP server authenticates clients with a long-lived static bearer token pasted into shared configuration files. Which redesign best follows MCP's authorization guidance for HTTP-based servers?
opts: Restrict the server to the office IP range and keep the static token, so that only trusted networks can use it
Make it an OAuth 2.1 resource server that points to its authorization server, with PKCE and short-lived, audience-bound tokens
Switch the transport to stdio and keep the token in the configuration so that it is never sent over a network
Rotate the static token every year and store it in a secrets vault that only the server team can read
why: The specification builds authorization on OAuth 2.1: the server publishes where its authorization server is, clients use PKCE and name the target resource, and tokens are short-lived and bound to the server. Network allowlists and yearly rotation keep a shared static secret, and stdio is a local-process transport that does not apply to a remote shared server.

q: A Managed Agents product lets each of 5,000 end users connect their own third-party accounts. The agent must act with the right user's access in each session without storing secrets in the agent definition. What is the best design?
opts: A single shared service credential embedded in the agent's system prompt, so every session can reach the services
One vault per user holding that user's credentials, referenced by its ID when each session is created
Each user's token passed in every message so that the model can forward the right one to each tool
A separate agent definition per user with that user's credentials baked into the agent's configuration
why: Vaults register a user's credentials once and are referenced by ID at session creation, so agent definitions stay reusable and secret-free and each run acts as the right person. A shared credential removes per-user attribution, tokens in prompts expose secrets to the model and logs, and per-user agent definitions multiply configuration and still embed secrets.

q: A single-page web app calls the Claude API directly from the browser with an API key in its JavaScript bundle. A security review rejects this. What is the best remediation?
opts: Obfuscate the key inside the bundle so that it cannot be read easily by anyone inspecting the page source
Restrict the key by HTTP referrer header so that it only works for requests from the app's own domain
Rotate the key weekly and keep it in the bundle, so any leaked value is only useful for a few days
Route requests through a back end that holds the credentials, authenticates users and applies per-user limits
why: Any secret shipped to a browser is public, and a referrer header can be forged. A back-end service keeps the credential server-side and is the right place to authenticate users, authorize what they can ask and apply rate and spend controls. Obfuscation and rotation do not remove the exposure.

q: A multi-tenant assistant exposes a search_documents tool over one shared index. A red team shows that a crafted message can make the model request another tenant's documents. Which control is the most robust?
opts: Instruct the model in the system prompt never to return other tenants' documents, whatever the user asks
Apply the caller's tenant filter inside the retrieval service, using the authenticated identity, so the model cannot widen it
Scan every answer with an output filter for other tenants' names and withhold any answer that matches
Deploy a separate model endpoint for each tenant, so each tenant's prompts and answers stay separate
why: Authorization must be enforced where the data is, using an identity the model cannot alter: the retrieval service filters by the authenticated tenant whatever arguments the model sends. Prompt instructions and output filters are probabilistic or after-the-fact, and separate model endpoints do nothing about a shared index.

q: A regulated organization requires that AWS be the sole data processor, wants IAM-based access control and must operate in an environment aligned to FedRAMP High. Which way of using Claude best fits?
opts: Claude Platform on AWS, billed through AWS Marketplace and authenticated with AWS IAM
The first-party Claude API reached over a private network link from the organization's AWS network
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs on AWS-operated infrastructure inside the AWS security boundary
Claude in Microsoft Foundry hosted on Anthropic, with access controlled through Microsoft Entra ID
why: Claude in Amazon Bedrock runs on AWS-operated infrastructure with AWS as the operating party, which is the offering Anthropic's guidance points to for FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 or HIPAA-ready needs and for AWS as sole processor. Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic, so Anthropic is the processor; the first-party API and a Foundry deployment hosted on Anthropic are Anthropic-operated too.

q: A product team buys everything through AWS Marketplace and needs Agent Skills, the MCP connector and batch processing. Legal has approved Anthropic as the data processor. Which option fits best?
opts: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which AWS operates and releases new features for on its own schedule
Claude on Google Cloud, using a regional endpoint for data residency and Google Cloud billing
Claude Platform on AWS, which Anthropic operates with AWS authentication and Marketplace billing
Claude in Microsoft Foundry hosted on Azure, billed through the Azure Marketplace in Claude Consumption Units
why: Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic's own platform reached through an AWS account, with AWS identity and Marketplace billing and typically same-day access to API features such as Skills, the MCP connector and batch processing. Bedrock and Google Cloud follow their own release schedules and do not offer those features, and a Foundry deployment hosted on Azure lacks Skills and is billed through Azure.

q: A team on Amazon Bedrock must guarantee that inference for EU customers happens only within the EU and accepts a modest price premium. Which endpoint choice fits?
opts: The global endpoint, because it routes each request to the nearest available region automatically
The global endpoint, plus a system prompt line stating that the data must remain in the EU at all times
A regional endpoint or an EU inference profile instead of the global endpoint, accepting the price premium
Any endpoint, since all Bedrock traffic stays within the customer's home country by default
why: Global endpoints route dynamically across regions for availability, so they give no residency guarantee. Regional endpoints (or a geography-scoped inference profile such as the EU one) pin processing to the chosen region or geography, at roughly a ten percent premium over global. A prompt cannot constrain where inference runs.

q: After creating a Claude deployment named finance-claude in a Foundry resource, requests with model set to claude-sonnet-5-5 fail with a model or deployment error. What is the most likely fix?
opts: Send a dated Anthropic model ID, since the deployment expects the full versioned name of the model
Create the deployment again in a different Azure region, where the model alias is registered
Pass the deployment name, finance-claude, as the model value in every request sent to that resource
Replace the Foundry key with a Bedrock bearer token, since model names are resolved by the cloud provider
why: In Foundry the deployment you create is what the API addresses: the deployment name goes in the model parameter. The default name matches the model ID, which hides this until you choose a custom name. Region and credentials from other platforms are not the cause.

q: One back-end service calls a single internal billing REST API in a deterministic step of a workflow, and no other AI client needs that integration. Which integration mechanism is most appropriate?
opts: Build and operate a dedicated MCP server for the billing API so that the integration follows an open standard
Call the billing API directly from the workflow code in that step, with ordinary service credentials
Delegate to a separate agent that wraps the billing API and returns the results to the workflow
Reach it through the Messages API MCP connector so that the model can call it as a remote tool
why: For one known system called from deterministic code, a direct API call is the simplest, most predictable choice. A protocol server pays off when several clients or agents must share an integration with consistent authentication. Wrapping the API in another agent or routing it through the connector adds moving parts with no benefit here.

q: Six AI clients (two IDE assistants, a chat app, a support agent and two batch jobs) all need the same CRM access with consistent authentication and per-user permissions. Which approach is best?
opts: Write a custom connector inside each client, tailored to that client's own plugin or extension mechanism
