Add a second model that must agree with the first, and drop human review whenever the two models give the same answer on a claim
Keep review for high-value or flagged claims, and sample a random, risk-weighted slice of auto-approved ones to measure the error rate
Hire enough reviewers to keep checking every claim indefinitely, because any reduction in review adds risk to the business and its customers
why: Review sampling replaces opinion with measurement: a random, risk-weighted sample of released outputs estimates the real error rate, catches drift, and gives leadership a defensible basis for loosening or tightening oversight, while high-value or flagged cases still get full review. Self-reported confidence is unvalidated, two models can share blind spots, and checking everything does not scale and invites rubber-stamping.

q: Reviewers approve 99 percent of AI-drafted loan summaries, each in under ten seconds. An audit finds material errors in 4 percent of the approved summaries. Which change best targets the underlying problem?
opts: Show the source evidence beside each recommendation, seed known-bad items into the queue, and track overrides and time per item
Email the reviewers a reminder that every summary must be read carefully before approval, and ask team leads to repeat it at the weekly meeting
Have the model add a 'high confidence' label to each summary so that reviewers can prioritize their time on the less certain ones
Replace the reviewers with a second model that rechecks each summary, since people are not catching errors
why: Approving 99 percent in seconds is automation bias: reviewers over-trust output that is usually right. The fix is to change the conditions of review: put evidence next to each recommendation, inject known-bad items to measure whether reviewers catch them, and watch override rates and time per item. A reminder email changes nothing structural, a model's own confidence label invites more trust, and a second model removes the accountable human instead of repairing the process.

q: An insurance Q&A agent should hand off to a person when it is unsure. The prototype asks the model to append a 0-100 confidence score and escalates below 70, but early data shows many wrong answers carry scores above 90. What is the best next step?
opts: Raise the threshold to 95 and keep the same design, since most of the wrong answers score in the nineties and a stricter cutoff catches them
Add a prompt line asking the model to be more honest about how confident it really is in each answer, and to say so when it is unsure
Remove the escalation path and rely on customer complaints to reveal which answers were wrong
Escalate on checkable signals (failed validator, weak retrieval support) and calibrate any confidence score against ground truth
why: A self-reported score is unvalidated, and here it demonstrably fails to separate right from wrong. Escalation rules should key on signals the system can check, such as validators, retrieval support, policy flags and amounts, and any confidence number must earn its place by being calibrated against labeled outcomes. A higher threshold or a request for honesty keeps the same unreliable signal, and waiting for complaints turns customers into the detector.

q: A lender wants a Claude-based assistant to recommend approve or decline for consumer credit applications, with staff handling exceptions only. Which design best matches Anthropic's usage policy for high-risk recommendations?
opts: Let the assistant decide automatically, and publish a general privacy notice on the lender's website with a link to the complaints process
Have a qualified loan officer meaningfully review each recommendation with authority to change it, and tell applicants that AI was used in producing the recommendation
Add a step in which the model checks its own recommendation for fairness, then release the result without review
Explain the model's reasoning to the applicant after the decision, which satisfies the policy without needing a person in the loop for each case
why: Credit is one of the high-risk areas in Anthropic's usage policy. For a recommendation there, a qualified person must meaningfully review it and be able to change it, and the affected individual must be clearly told that AI was involved. A privacy notice is not disclosure of AI use, a self-check is not human review, and an after-the-fact explanation provides neither the review nor timely disclosure. Check the current policy text and local law for the exact scope.

q: A European retailer will use Claude to summarize support chats that contain names, addresses and order numbers. The summaries feed a search index that is kept for years, and legal wants erasure requests to be honored. Which design is best?
opts: Send raw chats and rely on a zero data retention arrangement to satisfy erasure requests for the search index, because Anthropic then holds nothing about the customer
Store full raw chats in the index for better retrieval, and search the free text for the customer's name whenever an erasure request arrives
Redact or pseudonymize identifiers before the call, store only needed fields with a retention period, and keep a customer key for deletion
Keep all chats and summaries indefinitely, and tell customers that deletion is not technically possible, a common limitation of AI systems
why: Minimization and erasure are design properties you build in: send and store only what the task needs, replace identifiers with pseudonyms, set retention periods, and keep a key that links a person to every place their data lives so deletion is possible. Zero data retention concerns what Anthropic stores after the API response; it does not touch your own index or logs. Searching free text for a name misses variants, and refusing deletion on technical grounds is not a compliance position. This is general compliance practice; confirm specifics with counsel.

q: A health-tech company will send clinical notes (protected health information) to the Claude API and use structured outputs. The same organization also runs a marketing chatbot that uses code execution and the Files API. Which plan is correct?
opts: Enable HIPAA readiness with a signed agreement for the PHI organization, keep PHI out of schema definitions, and use a separate organization for marketing
Enable HIPAA readiness in the shared organization now, and switch it off later for the marketing features if the API blocks them, since an administrator can disable it
Enable zero data retention as well as HIPAA readiness, and put patient identifiers in enum values so that the schemas are descriptive and easy for reviewers to read
Skip the agreement, because encrypting prompts in transit is enough for protected health information under standard commercial terms
why: HIPAA readiness is an organization-level arrangement: it needs the signed business associate agreement, an administrator cannot disable it once it is enabled, and the API rejects requests that use features outside coverage (for example code execution). The marketing workload that needs those features therefore belongs in a different organization. Schema definitions are cached separately from message content and do not get the same PHI protection, so patient information must stay in message content. Zero data retention is an alternative arrangement, not an add-on, and transport encryption is no substitute for the agreement.

q: A legal-tech firm has zero data retention on its API organization. It plans to process 200,000 documents overnight at a lower price and wants them kept out of Anthropic's storage. A colleague proposes the Batch API. What should the architect conclude?
opts: Batch is covered by the arrangement, because the results are deleted as soon as the job's output has been downloaded, so nothing remains stored
Batch is fine, because zero data retention applies automatically to every Messages API feature and endpoint, so no feature-level checks are needed
Batch can be used only after HIPAA readiness has also been enabled for the organization and an agreement signed with Anthropic's legal team
Batch is not eligible for zero data retention because it stores jobs asynchronously; using it takes that data outside the arrangement
why: The feature eligibility table lists batch processing as not eligible: the service must store requests and results for a documented period so that jobs can run asynchronously. Nothing blocks the request, so the risk is silent: using it is a choice to step outside the arrangement for that data. If the documents must stay covered, use synchronous calls (with caching and sensible concurrency) and accept the higher price. Batch is not HIPAA-eligible either, so enabling that arrangement would not help.

q: A team under a zero data retention arrangement calls Claude Fable 5.1 and receives a 400 invalid_request_error saying the organization or workspace must have data retention enabled. Which resolution is correct?
opts: Retry the request with a different API key from the same workspace, since the error is specific to one key and the other keys may not be blocked
Resend the request through the Batch API, which has no retention requirement for these models and costs less per token than synchronous calls
Enable 30-day retention on one non-default workspace and send the Covered Model calls from it, leaving other workspaces unchanged
Wait a few minutes and retry, because the error is a transient capacity problem that clears by itself
why: Claude Fable 5.1 is one of the Covered Models, which require 30-day data retention and are not available under zero data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it; a request from an organization or workspace that does not meet this returns a 400. The documented path is to turn on standard retention for one workspace other than the Default Workspace (which follows the organization's setting) and use it for those calls. A new key does not change a workspace's retention, the Batch API is itself outside zero data retention, and a 400 is not transient.

q: A fintech must guarantee that inference for its regulated workload runs only on US infrastructure. Developers occasionally forget to set the per-request geography parameter. How should the architect enforce the rule?
opts: Ask developers to include the geography parameter on every request, and review the code every quarter to catch any request that omits it
Put the workload in its own workspace with allowed inference geos limited to the US and the default inference geo set to the US
Create the workspace with an EU workspace geo so that stored data stays closer to the customers and the European regulator that supervises them
Leave routing global and audit the inference geography reported in each response afterwards, escalating any request that ran outside the US
why: The per-request parameter depends on every developer remembering it. Workspace settings turn the rule into policy: restricting the allowed geos makes a request for any other geo fail, and setting the default means an omitted parameter still lands in the US. Workspace geo (where data is stored at rest) is a separate setting, fixed at creation and currently US only, so an EU option does not exist. Auditing responses detects a violation after the data was processed. US-only inference is priced at 1.1 times the standard rate on Claude 4.6 and later models, which belongs in the cost model.

q: A federal contractor must run its Claude workload under a FedRAMP High authorization. Which statement best guides the platform choice?
opts: Enable HIPAA readiness on the first-party API, since that arrangement also covers government security baselines such as FedRAMP and DoD impact levels
Enable zero data retention, which counts as the equivalent of holding a FedRAMP High authorization
Use any deployment as long as prompts are redacted, since FedRAMP concerns the data rather than the service
Anthropic's docs direct organizations needing FedRAMP High to Claude in Amazon Bedrock, where AWS operates the service; confirm status first
why: FedRAMP authorizes a cloud service at a Low, Moderate or High impact baseline, so the workload must run on a service that holds the required level. Anthropic's platform documentation points organizations that need FedRAMP High (and similar government baselines) to Claude in Amazon Bedrock, with AWS as the operating party. HIPAA readiness and zero data retention are different arrangements that confer no FedRAMP authorization, and redacting prompts does not change which service processes them. Verify the current authorization with the provider before committing.

q: An auditor asks who approved an AI-assisted decision six months ago and which prompt and model produced the draft. The team logged only the final decision. What should the audit trail have captured?
opts: Prompt and model versions, inputs, tool calls, the reviewer's decision and identity, and timestamps, in tamper-resistant, time-limited storage
Only the final decision and a user id, because storing prompts creates a privacy risk that outweighs any audit value for a routine decision like this one
Complete raw prompts and customer records in the ordinary application log, kept indefinitely so that nobody ever has to ask for them again
A weekly export of the dashboard's summary charts, showing overall volumes, approval rates and average handling time for the period, reviewed by the team lead
why: An audit trail must let you reconstruct and justify a decision later: who or what acted, when, with which inputs, prompt and model versions, tool calls and approvals, kept long enough and protected from tampering. A decision-only log cannot show which prompt or model produced the draft, keeping everything forever in ordinary logs conflicts with data minimization and retention limits, and charts aggregate away the individual case. Where full text is not needed, store references or hashes of sensitive inputs.

q: A Claude Enterprise security team wants to block prompts that contain unreleased financial results before the model sees them, and also to pull a history of who used Claude with which projects. Which pairing fits?
opts: The Compliance API for both, because it covers governance end to end, including blocking prompts before inference
Inference hooks for the inline allow or deny check, and the Compliance API for after-the-fact activity records
Inference hooks for both, because each hook verdict also stores a searchable record of who used Claude in the past
Access Transparency for the inline check, and inference hooks for the history of who used Claude with which projects
why: The two tools work at different moments. An inference hook sends each governed prompt to your own security server and waits for an allow or deny verdict before inference runs, so it can block. The Compliance API retrieves records afterwards (activity feed, users, chats, sessions) and blocks nothing. Access Transparency is a different record altogether: it logs human access to content by Anthropic personnel.

q: A legal-research assistant occasionally cites cases that do not exist. Lawyers rely on it for first drafts. Which approach best reduces this failure mode while keeping accountability?
opts: Tell the model in the system prompt never to invent citations and to double-check every case name, then trust the instruction to hold in production
Switch to the largest model tier, on the grounds that it does not hallucinate when it works on legal text
Ground answers in retrieved sources, require a checkable quote per claim, allow 'I don't know', verify quotes in code, and keep attorney review
Lower the randomness setting so that the model sticks to its most likely wording in every answer
why: Hallucination is a known failure mode that can be reduced but not eliminated. Anthropic's guidance combines grounding in provided documents, direct quotes and citations that can be checked, permission to say it does not know, and verification, and for high-stakes work a professional stays accountable. An instruction alone is guidance, no model is immune, and lower randomness makes wording more predictable without making facts true.

q: An agent reads inbound emails on behalf of trusted employees and can draft replies, forward messages and update records. Which three measures best reduce the risk from indirect prompt injection? (Choose three.)
opts: Deliver email text only inside tool results, JSON-encoded and labeled with its source, and state in the system prompt that such content is data and never instructions
Give the agent only the tools the job needs, and require approval before it forwards messages or changes records
Screen tool outputs with a small classifier, and withhold or summarize content flagged as containing instructions
Place the email text in the system prompt so that it carries the same priority as company policy
Show users a banner saying the assistant can be fooled, and leave the tool set unchanged
why: Structure (untrusted text only in labeled, encoded tool results, plus an untrusted-content policy), least privilege with approvals, and screening of tool output are the layered defenses for the trusted-user, hostile-content case. System-prompt placement gives hostile text the highest trust, and a banner informs users without reducing what a successful attack can do.

q: Which two statements about HIPAA readiness for the Claude API are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Once it is enabled for an organization, an administrator cannot switch it off
The API returns a 400 error when a request uses a feature outside coverage, such as code execution
It must be combined with zero data retention before protected health information may be sent
It can be turned on for a single workspace, so that PHI and non-PHI workloads can share one organization
It also covers Claude on Amazon Bedrock and prompts typed into the Console playground
why: HIPAA readiness is enforced at the organization level, is permanent once enabled, and is backed by API-side rejection of features outside coverage so that a team cannot use them by accident. It is an alternative to zero data retention for PHI, not an add-on, it cannot be scoped to one workspace, and it does not extend to partner platforms (which have their own compliance terms) or to Console usage.

q: Which three Claude API features keep data outside a zero data retention arrangement because they are stateful? (Choose three.)
opts: Batch processing, which stores requests and results so that jobs can run asynchronously
The Files API, which keeps uploaded files until they are deleted or expire
Code execution, which runs in containers whose data is retained for a period
Prompt caching, which holds cache representations in memory only for the cache lifetime
Token counting, which returns a count for a prospective request
why: Features that must store customer data to work (batch jobs, uploaded files, code execution containers) are marked not eligible in the feature eligibility table, and nothing blocks their use, so choosing one is a deliberate step outside the arrangement. Prompt caching holds only cache representations in memory for the cache lifetime, and token counting is eligible. Always confirm against the current table and your contract.

q: Before launching an agent that reads customer documents and calls tools, which three practices make red teaming worthwhile? (Choose three.)
opts: Test with hostile documents, emails and tool outputs against the real tool configuration
Keep a fixed attack set and rerun it on every release to see whether attacks succeed more or less often
Check that the screening and approval steps catch what the model itself ignores or misses
Run the tests once at launch against a stripped-down configuration with no tools attached
Use only polite, benign prompts so that results stay comparable across releases
why: Red teaming is adversarial testing of the system as it will run: hostile content against the actual tools, a stable attack set that measures regression release after release, and verification that the non-model layers (screens, approvals) catch what the model does not. A test without the real tools measures nothing about the blast radius, and benign prompts cannot reveal an attack path.

q: Which two practices keep human review of AI output meaningful rather than a rubber stamp? (Choose two.)
opts: Give reviewers the authority and the time to change or reject output, and show the supporting evidence beside it
Seed known-bad items into the queue, and track overrides and time per item to spot rubber-stamping
Set a quota that every reviewer must approve at least 95 percent of items to keep throughput high
Hide the model's sources from reviewers so that they are not anchored by the machine's reasoning
Place a reviewer at every step of the workflow, including trivial and easily reversible steps
why: Review is a control only if reviewers can actually change outcomes and have what they need to judge them; seeded errors and override statistics show whether they do. Approval quotas pressure reviewers toward agreement, hiding sources removes the evidence they need, and reviewing every trivial step produces fatigue that weakens attention where it matters.

q: A hiring-support assistant summarizes applications for recruiters. Which two actions best test it for unequal treatment? (Choose two.)
opts: Measure accuracy, error and refusal rates separately for each relevant subgroup
Run counterfactual pairs that differ only in a protected attribute or a likely proxy, and compare the results
Strip names from the inputs, then treat the matter as closed because the attribute is gone
Report the overall accuracy on the full test set and compare it with the vendor's benchmark
Ask the model in the prompt to ignore protected characteristics, and trust it to comply
why: Disaggregated evaluation exposes unequal performance that an overall average hides, and counterfactual pairs isolate the effect of a single attribute or proxy. Removing names leaves proxies such as schools, addresses or phrasing, an overall number averages the problem away, and a prompt instruction is an assumption rather than a measurement. Employment is also a high-risk area, so a qualified person must review recommendations and applicants must be told that AI was used.

q: When a harmlessness-screen call to a small Claude model returns a normal HTTP 200 response whose stop reason is 'refusal' and which contains no classification, the application should treat it as a harmful verdict rather than as a pass.
opts: True
False
why: The models' safety classifiers can decline the screening request itself, which leaves no verdict to read. Anthropic's guidance is to treat that outcome as a harmful verdict (fail closed). A refusal is a successful response, not an HTTP error, so code that only checks status codes would miss it and let the message through.

q: Even though Claude is trained to resist prompt injection, model behavior alone is not a sufficient security control for an agent that reads untrusted content and holds powerful tools.
opts: True
False
why: Resilience lowers the odds of a successful attack but does not remove it, so designs must limit what a fooled agent can do: smallest tool set, credentials kept out of its reach, sandboxing and approvals. Anthropic's own secure-deployment guidance makes the same point.

q: A zero data retention arrangement with Anthropic also keeps customer data out of the application's own logs, caches and search indexes.
opts: True
False
why: Zero data retention covers what Anthropic stores at rest after the API response is returned. Whatever your own application writes to logs, vector indexes, caches or analytics stores is your responsibility, so retention, access and deletion there must be designed separately.

q: Under zero data retention, Anthropic never retains prompts or responses under any circumstances, even when content is flagged by its safety systems or covered by a legal requirement.
opts: True
False
why: Retention is limited, not impossible: Anthropic may still retain data where the law requires it or where its automated trust and safety systems flag content (inputs and outputs of a flagged chat or session can be kept for up to two years). Architects should not promise stakeholders an absolute guarantee.

q: The first-party Claude API offers only US and global values for inference geography, so that parameter cannot by itself guarantee EU-only inference.
opts: True
False
why: Inference geo accepts global (the default) or us, and workspace geo, which governs storage at rest, is currently US only. A requirement for EU-only processing therefore calls for evaluating a partner platform whose regional endpoints or inference profiles can meet it, and for confirming the contract terms.

q: Customer-managed encryption keys protect data written after the key takes effect; data written earlier stays under Anthropic-managed keys.
opts: True
False
why: CMEK is not retroactive: existing data is not re-encrypted under your key, which is why Anthropic recommends attaching the key to a new workspace before any traffic. Enabling CMEK is permanent, and because Anthropic keeps no copy of the key, losing it destroys the protected data.

q: Access Transparency records each human view of covered customer content by Anthropic personnel, and automated safety processing does not generate such events.
opts: True
False
why: Access Transparency is an audit record of human access, permitted only under published reason codes and delivered through the Compliance API activity feed. Anthropic's automated safety systems process content in a pipeline without interactive human access, so they create no access events.

q: Removing names from a screening model's inputs is enough to show that it treats demographic groups fairly.
opts: True
False
why: Fairness has to be measured: proxies such as schools, locations, language or phrasing can still carry the attribute. Compare outcomes and error rates by group and use counterfactual pairs, then assign owners and fixes for any gap.

q: Telling the model in its system prompt to keep that prompt confidential is a dependable way to protect proprietary formulas placed in it.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's guidance is that no method is foolproof: keep unneeded proprietary detail out of the prompt, screen outputs for leaks, and use leak-resistance wording only when necessary because it can hurt task performance. A confidentiality instruction is guidance a determined user can often defeat.

q: A COO tells the architect, 'Put Claude on our claims inbox; I need a model choice and a date by next week.' Nothing else is documented. What should the architect do first?
opts: Pick the most capable model and build a demo on a handful of emails, then gather requirements from the reactions to the demo in follow-up meetings
Draft the full architecture from experience with similar clients and present it for sign-off together with a delivery date
Run structured discovery: map the workflow and volumes, find owners, data and error costs, record baselines, and agree success measures before any model is chosen
Start with the cheapest model and tune its prompt on the COO's examples until the COO says the answers look good
why: Discovery comes before design. The architect needs the problem statement, the current workflow and volumes, who decides and who can veto, what data is involved and how sensitive it is, what each kind of error costs, the constraints, and baseline numbers and success measures. A demo-first or model-first approach anchors the project on whatever the demo happens to show, a pre-written architecture hardens assumptions nobody has checked, and tuning on one executive's examples optimizes for a sample of one opinion. (Delivery practice.)

q: Stakeholders agreed that the assistant should 'answer accurately and quickly'. Six weeks into the build, security demands EU-only processing and legal requires an audit trail, and both change the design. Which discovery practice would have avoided this?
opts: Eliciting non-functional requirements explicitly (latency, accuracy, residency, retention, auditability) and naming security and legal in a RACI
Choosing a model with a larger context window, so that later requirements can be absorbed without a redesign of the architecture, the data flows or the hosting platform
Adding more reviewers to the team after launch, so that the extra compliance work is absorbed by people instead of by changes to the design and the project plan
Asking the model itself to list every regulation that might apply, and building to that list from the start of the project
why: Stakeholders rarely volunteer 'p95 under 3 seconds' or 'EU-only processing'. Discovery has to draw out the non-functional requirements and identify everyone with a veto (security, legal, compliance, operations) early, for example in a RACI matrix, because residency and audit needs change model choice, platform and architecture. A larger window, more reviewers or a model-generated checklist do not replace asking the people who own the constraints. (Delivery practice.)

q: A sponsor says the pilot will be approved 'if it feels good'. The architect wants a formulation that settles disputes with evidence. Which acceptance criterion is best?
opts: Reviewers should find the answers generally good by the time the pilot ends, as judged by the sponsor and the project team
The assistant should look clearly better than the previous prototype in most of the live demonstrations given to leadership and to the pilot team
Average satisfaction from the pilot team should be above four stars out of five in the end-of-pilot survey
95 percent of 500 representative cases correct, no critical-severity errors, p95 latency under 4 seconds, agreed before the build
why: Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, expressed as thresholds on a held-out evaluation set that mirrors real traffic, and agreed with the sponsor before the build so that the evaluation suite becomes the acceptance test. 'Generally good', 'looks better' and a friendly team's rating are opinions that cannot settle a dispute. Even softer topics such as safety can be quantified, for example as the share of outputs flagged in a large trial.

q: A sponsor wants a go decision. The proposal compares the monthly model bill with the staff hours saved if the assistant handles every ticket, yet in practice people will review 30 percent of the outputs. Which business case is most defensible?
opts: Show the monthly token bill against hours saved assuming full automation, using one optimistic figure so that the decision is easy to make
Show cost per completed task, including review time and running costs, against measured baselines, as a range with sensitivity analysis
Compare the model's price per million tokens with a competitor's price list and recommend whichever vendor is cheaper for the expected monthly volume
Postpone cost modeling until after launch, when the real invoices will make the numbers certain for everyone
why: A defensible case compares total cost of ownership per completed task, which includes model usage, retrieval and infrastructure, integration and evaluation work, human review time, monitoring, support and change management, with baseline numbers measured before the build. Present ranges and state the assumptions, because a single optimistic figure collapses when review rates or volumes differ. Token price alone is often a minority of the total in high-oversight workflows, and postponing the model leaves the sponsor deciding blind. (Delivery practice.)

q: A department head is alarmed that the assistant worded the same answer differently on two days, and demands that it behave 'like a calculator'. What is the best response?
opts: Promise that setting the sampling temperature to zero makes every output identical from one run to the next, so the behavior can be signed off by the department head this week
Explain that the variation is a defect that the vendor is expected to remove in an upcoming model release, and ask for patience until then
Explain that wording can vary between runs, agree which parts must stay stable, enforce them with schemas and validators, and measure consistency on an evaluation set
Replace generation with a fixed library of canned answers and stop using the model for this task altogether, accepting the loss of flexibility
why: Language models can word the same answer differently, which is a property to design around, not a bug to apologize for. Agree with the stakeholder what must be stable (facts, decisions, format), enforce structure with schemas and validators, and treat consistency as an acceptance criterion measured on an evaluation set. A promise of identical output cannot rest on a setting: recent models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values with a 400 error, and structured outputs guarantee schema conformance, not identical wording. Canned answers throw away the value of the solution.

q: Before a pilot of a clinical-documentation assistant, a skeptical physician asks, 'Can it be wrong?' Which way of setting expectations is best?
opts: Show measured error rates and types on representative cases, with real failures, and say which errors validation catches and which need review
Reassure the physician with the vendor's published benchmark scores for the model, including its results on medical knowledge and clinical reasoning tests
Say that errors are very rare because the testing was thorough, and offer to discuss the details with the physician after the pilot has ended
Show only the best demonstrations so that the physician sees what the assistant can do at its peak, then let the pilot reveal how it performs in everyday use
why: Expectation setting works when it is concrete and honest: show how often and in what ways the system is wrong on cases like the physician's own, which failures are caught automatically, and what the human must still check. General benchmarks do not describe this workload, reassurance without numbers invites distrust or over-reliance, and a best-case demo sets an expectation the system will break. For clinical content, review by a qualified person stays part of the design.

q: Eighteen months after launch, a new engineer asks why the team chose a mid-tier model, prompt caching and US-only inference, and proposes switching to a newer model. Which artifact best preserves the reasoning?
opts: The team chat history from the design period, which is searchable by keyword and shows who argued for each choice and when
The commit messages in the repository, which show when each setting changed and which engineer changed it
The system's model card, which describes its intended use, evaluation results by slice and known limits
A set of architecture decision records: context, options, criteria, the choice, consequences and when to revisit, kept beside the design
why: An architecture decision record captures one significant decision with its context, the options weighed, the criteria, the choice and its consequences, and a trigger for revisiting it, so the reasoning survives staff changes and can be re-run when a newer model ships. Chat history and commit messages hold fragments without the trade-offs, and a model card documents what the system is and where it fails, not why each design choice was made. (Delivery practice.)

q: Two architects disagree about using a workflow or an agent loop for a claims process, and each argues from personal experience. Which technique best moves the decision forward?
opts: Let the more senior architect decide, because experience is the fastest way to resolve a disagreement between two capable people
Agree weighted criteria with stakeholders first, score both options, then check whether the winner changes when the weights move, and record the decision in writing
Build both options in full and compare them with real traffic after launch before deciding which one to keep running
Take a vote among the engineers on the team and record the result as the decision, with a note of the dissenting views
why: A decision matrix turns preferences into explicit trade-offs: criteria such as accuracy, latency, cost, auditability and effort are weighted with stakeholders before any scoring, so nobody tunes the weights to favor a favorite, and a sensitivity check shows whether the conclusion is robust. Seniority and votes substitute authority or popularity for evidence, and building both in full spends the project's budget on the decision. (Delivery practice.)

q: Sales wants to promise customers 99.95 percent monthly availability for an assistant whose answer path depends on the Claude API on the standard tier, a vendor CRM and a search index. Which approach is most sound?
opts: Buy a Priority Tier commitment, which guarantees that the Claude API will be available whenever the assistant needs it, then promise 99.95 percent on that basis
Promise 99.95 percent and rely on service credits from the vendors if one of the dependencies fails
Base the commitment on the weakest dependency and your fallbacks, set an internal SLO tighter than the SLA, and promise no more than that supports
Offer no availability commitment at all, since model behavior cannot be guaranteed for any customer, and let each customer deal be negotiated separately
why: An SLA should promise only what the architecture and its least reliable dependency can sustain, backed by retries, queueing, cached or reduced answers and human handoff, with a tighter internal SLO as an early warning. The standard tier is best-effort, and new Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer sold; where one exists it targets uptime for committed capacity rather than guaranteeing it. Vendor credits do not repair a customer relationship, and refusing any commitment is rarely acceptable to customers.

q: A retailer will launch its assistant to two million customers on Monday after testing with 500 users. The expected peak is about forty times the test load, and the previous day's traffic will be near zero. Which plan best avoids a launch-day wave of 429 errors?
opts: Estimate peak requests and tokens against rate limits, ask for higher limits early, use caching, and ramp traffic in stages behind a feature flag
Rely on SDK retries with exponential backoff, and expect the extra attempts to absorb the surge as it builds during the first morning
Move the chat traffic to the Batch API, which has its own limits and a lower price per token, so launch-day load is spread over the day
Launch to everyone at once, so that the request for higher limits is justified by real demand and the provider sees the actual peak
why: Capacity planning compares expected peak requests and tokens with rate limits, spend caps and budgets before launch. Limits are maximums rather than guaranteed minimums, and a sharp jump from near-zero traffic can trigger acceleration limits that return 429 errors, so ramp gradually and ask for increases early. For most models, cached input reads do not count toward the input-token limit. Retries smooth short bursts but not a sustained overshoot, and batch processing is for latency-tolerant work, not live chat.

q: At 3 pm every request starts failing with HTTP 429. Request volume looks normal, the response carries no retry-after header, and the error body contains the code enforced_spend_limit_reached. What should the incident runbook conclude?
opts: A per-minute rate limit was exceeded, so the service should back off for a few seconds and retry the request, honoring the suggested delay
The API is overloaded across all users, so the service should wait for capacity to return and then resume sending traffic
An API key has expired, so the key should be rotated and the service redeployed with the new key after the security team has approved the change
The organization hit its tier's monthly spend cap, so retries fail until access resumes or the limit is raised; request an increase
why: A 429 with no retry-after header and the code enforced_spend_limit_reached means the organization has reached its tier's monthly spend cap. Usage stays paused until the first day of the next month (00:00 UTC) unless a higher limit is arranged, so backing off and the SDK's automatic retries cannot help. An ordinary rate limit carries a retry-after header, overload is a 529, and an expired key returns a 401. The runbook should cover raising the limit and alerting on spend well before the cap.

q: A pilot ran with the company's most enthusiastic power users and reported 94 percent satisfaction. The sponsor wants to roll out to 3,000 staff next month. What is the main weakness of the evidence?
opts: The pilot used too many users, so the satisfaction figure is too precise to be trusted and should be discarded in favor of a smaller sample
The group is unrepresentative and nothing was measured against a baseline or agreed thresholds, so results at scale will likely be worse
Pilots should run without human oversight, so that reviewers cannot influence the measured quality of the assistant's answers
Satisfaction is irrelevant to a rollout decision, because only the token cost per request matters when thousands of staff use it
why: Enthusiasts forgive flaws and use the tool well, so their satisfaction overstates what 3,000 ordinary staff will see. A pilot is evidence only if participants represent the real population and outcomes are compared with baseline numbers and acceptance criteria set beforehand. Extra oversight in a pilot is normal, satisfaction is one useful signal among accuracy, time saved and error severity, and cost is not the only measure. (Delivery practice.)

q: The plan moves the assistant from pilot to production on Friday. The evaluation suite still shows an unresolved class of critical-severity errors, but the sponsor is eager to ship. How does a phase gate help here?
opts: It lets the project ship on schedule and fix the critical errors during hypercare, because gates should never be allowed to delay a committed date
It lets the team lower the evaluation threshold until the suite passes, so that the planned date holds and the sponsor stays satisfied
Criteria agreed in advance make go or no-go a measurement: hold the release, or let the accountable owner record a formal risk acceptance
It lets the architect override the sponsor and cancel the project whenever any known error remains in the evaluation results
why: A phase gate checks agreed criteria (evaluation results, security review, operational readiness, budget) before work moves on, so the decision rests on evidence instead of enthusiasm. If a critical failure class is still open, the options are to hold, or for the accountable owner to accept the risk explicitly and on the record. Hypercare is for the tail of small issues, not for known critical errors; lowering the bar after seeing results defeats the gate; and a gate informs the decision rather than handing the architect a veto over the sponsor. (Delivery practice.)

q: The day before go-live, dashboards exist, but nobody is on call, rollback has never been tried and the incident runbook is a draft. What should the architect recommend?
opts: Treat the readiness review as not passed: assign on-call, test rollback and drill the runbook first, with early access limited to a small flagged cohort
Launch to everyone as planned, because the existing dashboards show that the system is being monitored well enough for a first release
Launch on schedule, and have the build team work out the rollback steps and the runbook if an incident actually occurs
Cancel the launch and restart discovery from the beginning, since operational gaps prove the original design was wrong
why: An operational readiness review is the last gate before go-live: monitoring and alerts, runbooks, on-call ownership, rollback, capacity, security sign-off, training and support must all exist. Dashboards without an owner, an untested rollback and a draft runbook mean nobody can respond when something breaks. The right move is to close the gaps (a limited, flagged cohort with hypercare can proceed once on-call and rollback work) rather than ship blind or discard the design. (Delivery practice.)

q: An email from Anthropic says the model your production service pins will be retired in about two months, and names a recommended replacement. Which plan is best?
opts: Wait until the last week, then change the model string, since the replacement is newer and will certainly be better than the model it replaces
Inventory usage, read the migration notes, adapt code and prompts, compare old and new on the evaluation suite, canary behind a flag, cut over early
Switch every environment to the largest available model today without testing, to be safe from any further retirements in the future
Ask support to postpone the retirement for your account, and plan nothing until they answer, so that no engineering time is spent meanwhile
why: A deprecated model keeps working until its retirement date, after which requests fail; Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for publicly released models and names a replacement. The plan is a migration, not a string change: find every use (the Console usage export breaks usage down by API key and model), read what changed for the replacement (rejected parameters, defaults, token counts), run your evaluations side by side, shadow or canary, and keep rollback ready. Waiting leaves no time to fix regressions, an untested jump to a bigger model risks cost and behavior surprises, and a postponement is not something to plan around.

q: A team moved a service from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5 by changing only the model ID. Some calls now fail with 400 errors, and the monthly cost is noticeably higher for the same traffic. What did the migration miss?
opts: Raising the organization's rate limits, since a shortage of capacity caused both the errors and the higher cost of the service
Wrapping every call in a retry loop, which resolves 400 responses and trims the cost of repeated attempts after each failed call
Removing settings the new model rejects (prefill, thinking budgets, non-default sampling), recounting tokens, setting effort, rerunning evaluations
Pinning the old model again for good, since newer models cannot run prompts that were written for earlier ones without being rewritten
why: Changing the model ID alone is rarely enough. Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns 400 errors for an assistant prefill and for a thinking token budget, and recent models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values; thinking now runs by default on requests that did not set it; and the same text produces roughly 30 percent more tokens than on Claude Sonnet 4.5, which raises cost and affects output limits. Retries do not fix a malformed request, rate limits are unrelated, and going back is only a short bridge because the old model has a published retirement date.

q: A support assistant's quality dropped on Tuesday. Its prompt lives in a database row that three people edit in an admin console, and nothing records who changed what or when. Which practice would have made diagnosis and recovery fast?
opts: Forbidding any prompt change after launch, so that the prompt can never be the cause of a quality drop, and requiring a director to approve exceptions
Tracking only daily token usage per request type, since a quality drop always shows up as a visible change in usage
Adding more reviewers to the support team, so that a quality drop is noticed sooner the next time it happens to a customer, and sharing the findings in a weekly report
Managing prompts, templates and settings as reviewed, versioned artifacts, with a release tag logged on every request and rollback available
why: Prompts are production code. With versioned, reviewed and tested prompts, a release tag recorded on every request and a rollback path, a Tuesday drop can be tied to a specific change within minutes and reverted. Editing live text in place leaves no history, a freeze blocks needed fixes, token usage does not measure answer quality, and more reviewers improve detection but not diagnosis. (Delivery practice.)

q: A harmful answer from the public chatbot is spreading on social media. Which response plan best fits a prepared incident runbook?
opts: Triage severity, contain with a flag or kill switch, update stakeholders, trace the cause via request IDs and logged versions, fix, add a regression case
Delete the related logs to limit what can be shared any further, and wait for the attention to fade before saying anything
Publicly state that the model vendor is responsible for the answer, and change nothing until the vendor replies
Deny that the answer came from the product until the investigation has been completed in full and approved by legal counsel
why: A prepared runbook turns panic into steps: assess severity, contain the behavior quickly (a feature flag or kill switch is why you keep them), tell stakeholders the facts and the actions, find the cause using the request IDs and the prompt and model versions logged on every request, fix, add the case to the regression set, and hold a blameless review. Deleting logs destroys the evidence you need, deflecting to the vendor ignores that the solution owner is accountable, and denial erodes trust when it is disproved. (Delivery practice.)

q: An excellent internal assistant launched six months ago, but only 12 percent of the target staff use it, although the technical dashboards are green. What is the most likely gap and the best fix?
opts: The model is too weak, so the team should upgrade to the newest tier and relaunch the assistant with a company-wide announcement
Change management was missing: engage teams early, train them, name champions, open a feedback channel, phase adoption
Staff lack discipline, so usage should be mandated by policy and non-users reported to their managers each month
The assistant lacks features, so the team should add more tools and integrations before telling anyone about it again, this time with a bigger launch event
why: Technical success with unprepared users still fails. Adoption follows people's trust and habits: engage the affected teams early, train them on what the assistant does well and badly, name champions who share concrete wins, give them a place to report problems, phase the rollout and measure adoption alongside quality. Claude Code's champion and communications kits illustrate the pattern. Green dashboards say nothing about whether people use the tool, and upgrading, mandating or adding features addresses guesses instead of the cause.

q: Reviewers correct about 15 percent of the assistant's drafts, but the corrections vanish after sending. The sponsor asks how quality will improve over time. What is the best feedback loop?
opts: Run a quarterly satisfaction survey of all staff and share the results with the team in a slide deck at the next planning meeting
Expect the assistant to learn from the reviewers' corrections automatically between conversations, because it sees every edit that is made
Capture each correction with its input, draft and reason code in an evaluation set, and review it on a schedule to drive changes
Ask reviewers to write free-form notes in a shared document, and read the notes at the annual review of the project
why: A feedback loop needs captured, structured signals and a cadence that turns them into action. Reviewer corrections are the best labeled data you will get: stored with context and a reason they become the evaluation set and the backlog for prompt, retrieval or tool changes, and trend reports keep sponsors aligned. The model does not learn between conversations by itself, surveys are too coarse, and unstructured notes read once a year are lost.

q: Three months after launch, accuracy on sampled production traffic has slipped from 94 to 89 percent although no code changed. Which lifecycle practice detects and handles this best?
opts: A yearly architecture review that revisits the original design assumptions with the whole team
Waiting for complaints to arrive, since users are the best detectors of any loss of quality in a deployed assistant
Redeploying the same release to reset it, then closing the ticket once the dashboards look normal again for a day
Monitor sampled quality against the acceptance thresholds, alert on a breach, investigate inputs and retrieval, and rerun the regression suite
why: Quality can drift without any code change: the mix of questions shifts, source documents are refreshed, or a dependency behaves differently. The monitoring and iteration phase samples production traffic, scores it against the acceptance criteria, alerts on a breach, diagnoses the cause and feeds a planned iteration. Annual reviews and complaints are too slow and incomplete, and redeploying the same release changes nothing.

q: The build team is handing a production assistant to operations. Which three items belong in the handoff package? (Choose three.)
opts: Runbooks for likely situations (a burst of 429 errors, a harmful output, a model retirement), tested in a drill
The evaluation suite, dashboards and alert thresholds, with prompt and model release tags recorded on every request
A named owner list with escalation contacts, a data-flow diagram, and system documentation covering intended use, limits and known failure modes
The build engineers' personal API keys, shared in a team document, so that operations can call the model in an emergency
A single verbal walkthrough of the design, because written documents go stale and nobody reads them
why: A handoff transfers the ability to operate, change and defend the system: tested runbooks, the evaluation suite and dashboards with release tags that tie behavior to versions, named owners and escalation paths, plus a data-flow diagram and a system document (a model card) that say what the system is for and where it fails. Sharing personal keys breaks identity and offboarding rules, and a one-time talk cannot be audited or repeated. (Delivery practice.)

q: Which two practices make a pilot's results a trustworthy basis for a rollout decision? (Choose two.)
opts: Choose participants who represent the real user population, not only enthusiastic volunteers
Measure outcomes against baseline numbers and acceptance criteria agreed before the pilot started
Define what counts as success after the results are in, so that the criteria fit what was achieved
Remove all human oversight during the pilot so that the raw performance of the model is visible
Limit the pilot to the team that built the assistant, because they understand its quirks best
why: A pilot is evidence only when the sample looks like the eventual users and the yardstick was fixed beforehand and compared with a measured baseline. Setting criteria after the fact lets the result define the test, removing oversight in a live pilot adds risk without adding insight, and the builders are the least representative users. (Delivery practice.)

q: Which two actions are part of change management for rolling out a Claude-based assistant to a large workforce? (Choose two.)
opts: Name champions in each team and give people a single channel for questions and feedback
Train users on what the assistant does well and where it can be wrong, and phase adoption by group
Announce the launch by email and measure success only by whether the servers stay up
Keep the assistant's limits out of communications so that users are not discouraged
Switch off the previous process on launch day so that nobody has a fallback
why: Change management is the people side of a rollout: champions and a visible feedback channel make adoption social and give problems a place to land, and honest training with phased adoption sets accurate expectations. Uptime says nothing about use, hiding limits sets users up for disappointment, and removing the fallback turns every flaw into an outage. (Delivery practice.)

q: Monitoring shows that a scheduled agent on Claude Managed Agents sent customer data to an unknown address after reading a poisoned ticket. Which three actions belong in the first response? (Choose three.)
opts: Interrupt the running session and pause the deployment, so that no new scheduled run starts
Rotate any key or credential the agent could use, at the service that issued it
Copy the session's events to your own logs before anything is archived or deleted
Delete the session straight away so that the poisoned ticket cannot be read again
Archive the agent definition, which also stops any of its sessions that are already running
why: Contain first: send an interrupt to the running session and pause the scheduled deployment so nothing new starts, then rotate any key the agent could reach, because an interrupt does not undo what it already did or sent. Preserve the session's events in your own logs before archiving or deleting, since deletion removes the record. Archiving an agent does not stop its running sessions, and a running session cannot be archived or deleted until it goes idle.

q: The Claude API intermittently returns overloaded errors during peak hours, and the assistant is customer-facing. Which three measures belong in the degradation plan? (Choose three.)
opts: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff, honoring any retry-after header
Serve cached or reduced answers, or queue work for later, and hand off to a person where needed
Tell users clearly when they are in a degraded mode, and test the fallback paths before launch
Retry immediately in a tight loop without limit until a call succeeds
Hide the degraded state from users so that confidence in the product is not shaken
why: Graceful degradation plans a reduced but acceptable experience for each failing dependency: bounded retries with backoff for transient errors, cached or reduced answers, queuing and human handoff as fallbacks, honest status messages, and tests that prove the fallbacks work before they are needed. Unbounded tight retries amplify the overload, and hiding the degraded mode misleads users.

q: For publicly released models, Anthropic notifies customers with active deployments at least 60 days before a model is retired.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's model deprecations page commits to at least 60 days' notice before retirement of publicly released models, by email and in the documentation. A deprecated model still works until its retirement date, after which requests fail, so the notice period is the planning window for migration.

q: Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud retire Claude models on the same dates as the first-party Claude API, so one retirement notice covers every deployment.
opts: True
False
why: The dates on Anthropic's deprecation page apply to Anthropic-operated platforms (the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry). Partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own retirement schedules, so the lifecycle owner must check each platform's model table separately.

q: New Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer sold, so an availability plan should not depend on buying one and should rely on retries, fallbacks and headroom instead.
opts: True
False
why: Existing commitments run to the end of their contract, but new ones are not offered, and the standard tier is best-effort. Design for transient overload with backoff, graceful degradation and spare capacity, and size any SLA to what that design can sustain.

q: A proof of concept that worked on real data can go to production as it is, because it already proved the idea.
opts: True
False
why: A proof of concept answers a few risky questions about feasibility and value, usually without evaluation depth, security review, monitoring, runbooks or support. Moving to production needs the later lifecycle phases: pilot, phase gates and operational readiness. (Delivery practice.)

q: An internal service level objective is usually set tighter than the external SLA, so the team is alerted before a customer commitment is at risk.
opts: True
False
why: The SLO is the working target (for example a share of answers within a time limit) and the SLA is the contractual promise with consequences. The gap is the early-warning margin, and an error budget derived from the SLO tells teams when to prioritize stability over new releases. (Delivery practice.)

q: The model usage bill is normally the complete cost of ownership of a Claude-based workflow.
opts: True
False
why: Total cost of ownership also includes retrieval and infrastructure, integration and engineering, evaluation, human review time, monitoring and support, and training and change management. In high-oversight workflows tokens are often a minority of the total, so a business case built on tokens alone misleads. (Delivery practice.)

q: Interrupting a running agent session undoes the actions it has already taken and recalls data it has already sent.
opts: True
False
why: An interrupt stops further model output (a running tool call may still finish), but it cannot reverse completed actions or recall data that has been sent. Incident response therefore also rotates credentials, pauses schedules, preserves evidence and assesses the impact.

q: A feature flag lets a team switch a prompt version or model on for chosen users or percentages without redeploying, and doubles as a kill switch for risky behavior.
opts: True
False
why: Flags separate deployment from release: a new prompt or model can be exposed to a canary share, compared on quality and cost, and turned off in seconds if something goes wrong, which is why flags appear in both rollout plans and incident runbooks. (Delivery practice.)

q: Because newer models can reject parameters that older code sets, moving to a new model needs a test against its migration notes, not just a changed model ID.
opts: True
False
why: Examples from the current migration guides: assistant prefill, thinking token budgets and non-default sampling values return 400 errors on recent models, defaults such as thinking can change, and token counts differ. Treat every model move as a small project with an evaluation run, not a configuration edit.

q: A bank's auditors require that developers on MDM-enrolled laptops cannot weaken the organization's Claude Code permission policy, even if they try. Which delivery mechanism best satisfies this?
opts: Endpoint-managed settings deployed through MDM (a profile, a registry policy or a protected file), which the operating system guards from user edits
Server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console, because the policy is fetched from Anthropic's servers and developers cannot see or change it
A .claude/settings.json file committed to each repository, with changes reviewed through pull requests by the platform team
An organization-wide CLAUDE.md that states the permission policy in plain language and is loaded into every session
why: Managed settings rank above user and project settings whichever route carries them, but the routes differ in strength. Server-managed settings are fetched at startup and refreshed hourly, which is convenient with no device management, yet they are a client-side control: a local cache can be edited until the next fetch and an older client may not fetch them at all. Settings placed on the device by MDM (or a protected system file) are guarded by operating-system permissions, so they give the stronger guarantee. Repository settings are not managed policy, and CLAUDE.md is guidance rather than enforcement.

q: A security team adds a managed deny rule for the WebFetch tool to stop Claude Code from sending data to arbitrary websites. A penetration test shows that Claude can still reach an external site by running curl through the Bash tool, which developers need for other work. What is the best remediation?
opts: Enable sandboxing with a network allowlist of approved domains, which the operating system enforces whatever command is typed
Add a line to CLAUDE.md telling Claude never to use curl or wget, and ask reviewers to scan session transcripts for network commands
Add an allow rule for Bash(curl https://approved.example.com *) so that curl may be used only for that one approved address
Remove the Bash tool from every developer's configuration, so that builds and test runs have to be started by hand
why: Permission rules match tool names and command text, so denying WebFetch removes only that tool; with Bash allowed, curl or wget can still reach any address, and Bash patterns that constrain arguments are fragile (extra options, other protocols, redirects, variables, wrappers such as sh -c). Sandboxing enforces filesystem and network limits at the operating-system level regardless of how a command is written. CLAUDE.md only shapes what Claude tries, and removing Bash contradicts the stated requirement.

q: To control spend, an administrator sets the model key to a mid-tier model in managed settings. Usage reports show that developers still run the most expensive tier by passing --model on the command line. Which managed setting actually restricts the choice?
opts: availableModels, an allowlist that limits which models developers can select
maxEffortLevel, which caps the effort level that sessions can use
modelPricing, which sets contracted per-token rates so that cost reporting matches the invoice
minimumVersion, which stops auto-update from installing an older release
why: A managed model value is only a default: --model and the model environment variable still choose the model for a session. availableModels is the restriction, and adding enforceAvailableModels also constrains the automatically selected default. maxEffortLevel limits how much thinking effort a session may use, not which model; modelPricing changes only the cost figures Claude Code displays, not what Anthropic charges or what developers may run; minimumVersion concerns client versions.

q: A team's CLAUDE.md says 'Run the linter after every file edit.' Claude Code usually complies but sometimes skips it, and the team's rule is that lint must run after every edit, with no exceptions. What is the best fix?
opts: Add the word IMPORTANT and repeat the instruction at the top and the bottom of CLAUDE.md so it is harder to overlook
Configure a PostToolUse hook on the editing tools that runs the linter after every edit, deterministically
Move the instruction into a skill so that it loads only when the current task looks relevant to it
Switch to a larger model, which follows long written instructions more reliably than a smaller one
why: CLAUDE.md and skills are guidance that the model may or may not follow; hooks are commands the harness runs at fixed lifecycle points, so a PostToolUse hook on the editing tools guarantees the action. Emphasis and repetition lower the odds of a skip without removing it (and a bloated file makes rules easier to lose), a skill is still instruction the model decides to apply, and a larger model improves compliance but offers no guarantee. When a rule must always hold, programmatic enforcement beats prompt-based guidance.

q: A developer wants Claude Code to implement a new API endpoint and then keep working unattended while they attend a meeting. What most improves the chance that the result is correct when they return?
opts: Add 'be careful and double-check your work before you finish' to the prompt, and ask Claude to explain its reasoning
Give Claude tests, a build or a linter it can run and read itself, and tell it to iterate until they pass
Switch to the highest effort level so that the first attempt is right and fewer iterations are needed overall
Approve each edit as it happens so that mistakes are caught immediately, before they can build on one another
why: Without something that returns a pass or fail signal, 'looks done' is the only evidence and the developer becomes the verification loop. A runnable check (tests, build, linter, a screenshot comparison) lets Claude iterate to a verified result and show evidence, and a Stop hook can enforce that the turn cannot end until the check passes. Exhortations carry no signal, higher effort improves reasoning but not verification, and approving every edit defeats the purpose of unattended work.

q: A lead asks new team members to use plan mode for everything and then complains that it slows people down. For which task is plan mode most worthwhile?
opts: Correcting a misspelled word in a README paragraph and a matching heading
Renaming one local variable that is used only inside a single function
Adding one log statement to an existing request handler to see a value
Adding single sign-on that touches several files in an auth module the engineer has not worked in before
why: Plan mode separates exploration and planning from editing: the agent reads the code and proposes changes for approval before touching any file. That overhead pays off when the approach is uncertain, the change spans several files or the code is unfamiliar, because it prevents expensive rework from a wrong direction. When the diff can be described in one sentence (a typo, a rename, a log line), asking Claude to make it directly is faster.

q: A platform team announced Claude Code in an all-hands email. A month later only 12 percent of developers have tried it. Which next step best reflects Anthropic's adoption guidance?
opts: Set a weekly session quota for each team and report the numbers to managers every Friday
Send a longer announcement that lists every feature, with links to the full documentation for each one
Require everyone to finish a half-day training course before they are granted access to the tool
Have engineers who already use it well share concrete prompts and wins in channels teams read, and pair with colleagues on a first task
why: Adoption of a developer tool rarely follows an announcement. It follows someone on the team using the tool well, sharing reusable prompts and wins where colleagues already read, answering questions in public and offering a short pairing session on a real task. Anthropic's champion kit describes this low-cost, habit-forming approach with a modest weekly time budget. Quotas create compliance without value, a longer feature list adds reading but no experience, and a mandatory course adds friction before the first success.

q: Leadership asks whether Claude Code is worth its cost. The organization is on a Claude Enterprise plan with the GitHub integration for analytics enabled. Which evidence from the analytics best supports an answer?
opts: The leaderboard of the ten most active users, which shows that the tool is in demand across the engineering organization
Total lines of code accepted, since more accepted lines of Claude-written code means more value delivered to the business
The suggestion accept rate alone, since a high rate shows that developers trust the output enough to keep it
Merged pull requests per active user and the share with Claude-assisted code, read beside existing engineering metrics
why: Contribution metrics tie usage to outcomes in your own codebase: pull requests per user as adoption grows, and the share of merged pull requests with Claude-assisted code, ideally read with measures the organization already trusts such as DORA metrics or sprint velocity. Anthropic describes these metrics as deliberately conservative, so they understate rather than inflate impact. A leaderboard shows who uses the tool, and lines accepted or accept rate are activity measures that can rise without any business benefit.

q: A company runs Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock. Finance wants per-developer token and cost figures in the company's own observability stack, in near real time, and the Claude Code analytics dashboard shows nothing for these developers. What is the best approach?
opts: Query the Claude Code Analytics API with an Admin API key to get per-user figures for the Bedrock deployment
Turn on Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export in managed settings, pointed at the company's collector; it works with every provider
Divide the monthly cloud invoice by the number of developers to approximate each person's usage
Enable server-managed settings, which stream usage to the admin console as developers work
why: When Claude Code runs through a cloud provider it does not send usage metrics back to Anthropic, so the analytics dashboard and the Claude Code Analytics API do not cover that usage. OpenTelemetry export (enabled with an environment variable, best pinned in managed settings) is provider-independent and is the option that streams per-user token, cost and tool metrics into your own stack in near real time; a gateway is the other route. Dividing the invoice yields no per-person data, and server-managed settings deliver policy, not usage.

q: A team wants Claude to review every pull request diff in continuous integration with no human present, and to fail the job when it finds a critical issue. Which setup is best?
opts: Start an interactive Claude Code session on the runner and script the keystrokes that answer each permission prompt
Run claude -p with the diff piped in, a minimal tool allowlist, a turn limit and JSON output the pipeline parses, with the key stored as a pipeline secret
Run claude -p with permission checks bypassed and no turn limit, so that no step can ever stall the pipeline waiting for approval
Commit an API key into the workflow file, so that runners can authenticate without any secret-store setup
why: Non-interactive mode is built for pipelines: it reads standard input, exits with a status code and can return structured output (--output-format json, optionally with --json-schema) that a later step parses to fail the job. Restricting tools with --allowedTools, capping iterations with a turn limit and keeping credentials in the secret store make the run safe, predictable and affordable. Scripting an interactive session is brittle, bypassing permissions with no cap removes the safeguards unattended runs need most, and a committed key is a leaked credential.

q: An on-call engineer wants Claude Code's help with an intermittent production failure. The relevant service wrote a 40,000-line log. What is the best way to use Claude?
opts: Paste the entire 40,000-line log into the prompt and ask Claude to read it all and find the root cause
Ask Claude to investigate the failing service with no further direction and let it read whichever files and logs it decides to
Filter the log to the failing window and error lines, then give Claude the stack trace, reproduction steps and a failing-test request
Give Claude write access to the production host so that it can try candidate fixes directly and observe what happens to live traffic
why: Context is the scarce resource. Pasting 40,000 lines wastes tokens and degrades performance, and an unscoped 'investigate' request lets the agent read hundreds of files. Preprocessing the log to the relevant lines (a script or hook can cut tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds) and supplying the symptom, the likely location and what 'fixed' looks like gives a focused diagnosis, while a failing test reproduces the issue before any fix. Direct write access to production bypasses review and safety controls.

q: Which two managed settings together stop developers from loosening the organization's permission policy on their own machines? (Choose two.)
opts: allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly set to true, so that permission rules from user, project and local files are ignored
permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to disable, which removes the mode that skips permission prompts
A deny rule in each repository's .claude/settings.json for the dangerous commands
An organization-wide CLAUDE.md line that forbids changing permission settings
A quarterly reminder in the onboarding guide to review user settings
why: Permission lockdown is managed-only configuration: the first key makes managed settings the only source of permission rules, and the second disables the bypass mode that skips prompts. Repository settings sit below managed policy and can be changed by anyone with write access, CLAUDE.md is guidance the model may not follow, and a reminder relies on goodwill rather than enforcement.

q: Developers use Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock. Which two routes can provide per-developer token and cost figures? (Choose two.)
opts: OpenTelemetry export from each developer's machine to the company's own collector
A gateway between Claude Code and Bedrock that tracks usage per developer credential
The Claude Code analytics dashboard at claude.ai
The Claude Code Analytics API called with an Admin API key
The Usage and Cost Admin API of the company's Claude API organization
why: Claude Code does not send metrics from a cloud-provider deployment back to Anthropic, so the Anthropic dashboard, the Claude Code Analytics API and the Usage and Cost Admin API (which report Anthropic-billed usage) do not see it. OpenTelemetry export works with every provider, and a gateway (Anthropic's self-hosted Claude apps gateway or another LLM gateway) attributes usage per credential. The cloud provider's own billing console covers spend in aggregate.

q: Which two practices keep Claude Code effective across a long working day? (Choose two.)
opts: Clear the context between unrelated tasks
After two failed corrections on the same issue, clear the context and restart with a more specific prompt
Keep one session open for the whole sprint, so that all history stays available
Add IMPORTANT to every line of CLAUDE.md, so that none of the rules is skipped
Paste complete build logs into each prompt, so Claude always has full information
why: Context fills quickly and performance degrades as it fills, so unrelated work should start fresh, and a session polluted by repeated failed corrections is better replaced by a clean one with a sharper prompt. Keeping everything in one session accumulates noise and cost, emphasizing every line means none stands out, and pasting whole logs wastes tokens that scoping or filtering would save.

q: A scheduled job runs claude -p unattended against the repository each night. Which three settings make it safer and cheaper? (Choose three.)
opts: Restrict --allowedTools to the tools the job actually needs
Cap the run with a turn limit (or a spend limit)
Store the API key as a pipeline secret rather than in the repository
Bypass all permission checks so that nothing can block the run
Let it load whichever hooks and MCP servers are configured on the runner, so that it behaves like a developer laptop
why: Unattended runs need least privilege (a minimal tool allowlist), a bound on work and spend (turn or budget limits) and protected credentials. Bypassing permission checks removes the safeguards exactly when nobody is watching, and loading whatever configuration happens to exist on the runner makes behavior depend on the machine; scripted runs are better with explicit configuration (bare mode skips that auto-discovery).

q: Claude Code applies managed settings above user and project settings, so a value in a repository's .claude/settings.json cannot override a managed value.
opts: True
False
why: Managed settings are the top tier whichever delivery route carries them (a few security-sensitive keys let a stricter lower-level value still count). Array settings such as permission rules merge, so developers can add entries but not remove managed ones.

q: Server-managed settings are a hard security boundary that developers on unmanaged devices cannot bypass.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic describes them as a client-side control, not a security boundary: on an unmanaged device a user can edit the cached copy until the next fetch, run an older client, or configure a different provider so that the fetch is skipped. Endpoint-managed settings protected by MDM give stronger guarantees.

q: A CLAUDE.md instruction guarantees that Claude Code will run a named command after every edit.
opts: True
False
why: CLAUDE.md is context that the model reads and usually follows, which makes it guidance, not enforcement. A rule that must always hold needs a hook (deterministic), a permission rule or a sandbox.

q: A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call even when the session is running in a permissive permission mode.
opts: True
False
why: PreToolUse hooks run before any permission-mode check, and a hook that exits with code 2 or returns a deny decision stops the call even in bypass mode. That is why hooks, especially managed ones, can enforce rules that individual developers cannot skip.

q: Claude Code's checkpoints restore files that were changed by shell commands Claude ran through the Bash tool.
opts: True
False
why: Checkpoints snapshot files before Claude's own file-editing tools change them. Changes made by shell commands (for example sed -i, rm or mv) or by external processes are not captured, so checkpoints complement version control rather than replace it.

q: The contribution metrics in the Claude Code analytics dashboard are deliberately conservative, so they tend to understate Claude Code's real impact.
opts: True
False
why: Only lines and pull requests where there is high confidence of Claude Code's involvement are counted, heavily rewritten code is not attributed, and sessions outside the attribution window are ignored. The metrics also exclude organizations with zero data retention and usage outside the claude.ai organization.
